div.head: WARRINGTON HORSE PARADE.
div.p: WARRINGTON HORSE PARADE.
A RECORD SHOW.

Warrington is justifiably proud of its annual horse parade which, from very small beginningi, has made such splendid progress that it can now hold its own with most displays of the kind in the industtial centres of England. Saturday's parade, which was the twelfth, far surpassed any of its predecessors in general excellence. It took place under ideal con- ditions, the brilliant sunshine adding just the necessary finishing touch to the scenes of animation witnessed in front of the Town Hall where the judging took place. Admirably groomed and gaily caparisoned, the horses were seen at their best and fine specimens most of' them were. One :tould not help contrasting the , parade with that first little venture of twelve years ago. The improvement was so complete and indeed remarkable, that satisfactory comparison was out of the question. What most happily impressed the spectator was the unmistakable evidence that the parade is achieving its main object of encouraging owners and drivers to take a real interest in the condition of their horses. Even a casual survey dis- closed the fact that the restilts achieved were not the result of any spasmodic or eleventb-hour effort to create a favourable impres,ion, but that the animals had been carefully looked after through- out the year. From the numerical stand- point alone, the parade marked a record, the entries numbering 158. as compared with 111 last year—an advance of 50 per cent. Not only were the horses in tbe pink of condition, but the smartness of the turnouts called forth general admiration. The

div.p: JUDGING AT THE HORSE PARADE ON SATURDAY. THE MAYORESS LOOKING ON.

lines on which the judging was conducted were such as to give every encouragement to the humble exhibi- tor, the general condition of the horse, its fitness for the work, and the cleanliness of the harness being the chief points considered. There was consequently no danger of the small tradeeman being placed in com- petition on unequal terms with large owners. The judging attracted a large glthering of leading townspeople to the Town Hall, and all were agreed that the parade realized the most sanguine expecta- tions. Among those present were :—Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. (president of the parade) and Lady Greenall, the Mayor and Mayoress, Mr. A. Nield, Mr. and Mrs. W. Peter Rylands, Mr. and Mrs J. Fulton Smith, Mrs. Greenall, Aldermen Smethurst, Tinnion sod Bennett, Councillors Bellian, Jenk ins and Jackson Holmes. The marshalling of the exhibits was carried out with the utmost expedition and smoothness. In this connection special praise is due to the police, tinder the direction of the Chief Constable (Mr. M. Nicholls). A contingent of mounted officers was on duty, and rendered very efficient service.

The judging wa, of a very thorough and critical character, each turnout being subjected to a minute examination. The committee are to be congratulated on securing the services of such well-known experts as Captain E W Griffith (Tarporley), Messrs Alfred Ashton (Tarporley), W D Bullock (Altrincham), II C Burder (Moore), It Flemming (London), C It Longa (ICnutsford), It B Neilson (Liverpool), and James Tinsley (Daresbury). In conversation with some of these gentlemen, our representative learned that they considered the parade extraordinarily good. One of the judges said he had officiated at Warrington for five years and during the whole of that time there had been a distinct improvement in the care of the animals. Although the number of first prizes was smaller than last year, it was not due to any falling off in quality but to the mote stringent standard which the judges had adopted. A feature which greatly impressed bins was the wonder- full way in which the collars of the horses were

ME LUNCHEON. On completion of the judging, the officials, judges and committee partook of luncheon at the Lion Hotel, Mr. John Lee catering admirably.

Sir GILBERT GREFNALL, Bart., who presided, pro- posed the health of" The Judges " to whom, he said, the committee owed a debt of gratitude for the time and care they had given to the work. It was gratify- ing to know that the judges had repeatedly expressed satisfaction at the great improvement in the quality of the exhibits which had been manifested since the parade was first instituted. The committee felt they had done great service to those people in Wsrrington who kept horses, by encouraging the drivers to take a greater interest in their charges. Sir Gilbert also coupled with the toast the name of the Chief Constable without whose ready assistance, he said, it would be impossible to carry on the parade in such an expeditious manner. (Applause).

Mr. IL FLEMMING, in responding,said he could safely say on behalf of all the judges that they enjoyed coming to Warrington as much as the committe appreciated their presence. They, in turn, learnt their lesson, for they found how everything in Warrington was done as thoroughly as possible—nothing being left to chance. (Applause).

The CHIEF CONSTABLE said the part which the police took in the parade vas a very small one, but they did their work to the beat of their ability and were only too pleased to be able to assist. They were not horse men but they were partially sportsmen and appreciated the splendid work that was being done by the parade. That was palpable even to a man who knew nothing about a horse except when he saw one running on the race- course. (Laughter.) He had been much impressed by the consid-rable improvement which had been effected in the condition of the horses of Warrington during the five years he hsd been connected with the town. - - - - —•--

Mr W D Bur-Locic proposed the health of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart , and referred to his interest in every- thing that conduced to the welfare of the town. If it were not for his help, they would not have such an excellent parade.

div.head: DANGEROUS ROAD.
div.p: A DANGEROUS ROAD.
Important Improvement Contemplated.
MR. COUGH'S QUESTIONS.

An improvement contemplated by the Corporation with the object of removing the danger which undoubtedly exists at the narrowest point of Knutsford- road, was under consideration at an inquiry held by Mr. F. H. Tulloch, an inspector of the Local Government Board, at the Warrington Town Hall on Wednesday, into the application of the Council for ssnction to the borrowing of £546 for the purchase of property in Knutsford-road. Amongst those present were : The Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph), Councillors T Birtles and CJazlsson Ilolmes,Mr W Throssell (on behalf of the Warrington and District Property Owners' Association), Mr S Gough, Messrs J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), T H Spinks (assistant town clerk), W 11 Woodcock (borough collector), and A M Ker (deputy-surveyor). The Town Clerk explained that the property was required in the first place for strect improvements. The road at the point in question was exceedingly narrow-30ft. in the narrowest part and 421 t. in the widest. The property consisted of two cottages and a strip of land. After passing the cottages there was no footpath on that side of the road. There were two sets of tram rails and the Corporation some time ago pre- scribed a street line through the cottages and land. Further along Knutsford-road tbe land between the river and the roadway narrowed and the road was highly dangerous at that point, because there was a drop into the river of many feet and at high water the river was about 20ft deep. The Borough Surveyor had reported that the road was dangerous, and in consiquence the Corporation included, io the Bill sanctioned by Parlia- ment last session powers to construct a river wall from Victoria Park to the end of the property it was now proposed to purchase. While the rcmn Clerk was explaining the plans in some detail

Mr Gough remarked : The information the Town Clerk is giving you is something which I am afraid the ratepayers have no knowledge of. The Town Clerk : I was only only telling the inspector that we shall have no land for re-sale when we have made the wall. Later Mr Cough asked if the Corporation was acquir- ing the property with the object of altering the position of the tram lines?
The Town Clerk : It is very probable that the tram lines will be altered some day when the road is widened.
Mr. Gough : Is the object to acquire this property for street improvement ? The Town Clerk : It is incidental. Mr. Gough: Is this road dangerous, with the double tram lines ?

The Town Clerk : Certainly. I have said so to the inspector. Air. Gough : Is it a fact that carts cannot deliver goods at the houses without drawing on to the footpath? The Town Clerk : That is correct. it shows the necessity of widening the road. Mr. Gough : Have the tram cars been damaged

Sir GILBRRT GREY:NALL, returning thanks' said he always looked forwardto the parade with great pleasure. The committe were doing an excellent work and he would always le ready to do all he could to assist them. They did not know what changes motor traction was going to effect, but so long as there were horses, the parade committee would help to look after them. (Applause). Sir GILBERT then proposed the health of the secre- tary (Mr A II Clive) and paid a high tribute to his tire- less work on behalf of the parad3. lie kept everything straight, succeeded in obtaining new subscribers every 1 year and in short, worked very hard indeed. (Applause.) Mr. CLIVE said he had thought he might be subject to some criticism instead of praise, seeing that each ' year he landed them in debt. (Laughter.) What little work to was able to do in connection with the parade he did very a illingly. He had received every assistance from the members of the committee, and particularly from Mr Venn, and his labours had thus been consider- ably lightened. They were, in fact, very light indeed with the exception ot a certain amount of detail work during the seek preceding the parade. So long as one saw an improvement being maintained end appreciation shown from year to year, there was ample encourage- ment to persevere in one's efforts to improve the parade in every respect. div.head: GREAT INSURANCE ACT.
div.p: THE GREAT INSURANCE ACT.
110 W 111 DEALS WITH UNEMPLOYMENT.
BY GODFREY P. COLLINS, M.P.

Admittedly one of the most difficult, un• employment insurance is at the same time an essential and even vital section of the National Insurance Act, for it cuts close to the roots of the gravest and most serious afflictions from which the country suffers. The dread of being suddenly thrown "out of a job" is the bane of many a workman'a existence, and anything tending to lessen that evil is a positive national asset. Ignorance of any subject naturally brae& ' distrust and encouralcs misrepresentation, but the more thoroughly unemployment in- surance is studied the more readily will it be , admitted that this is a courageous, intelligent, and successful effort to deal with the misery attendant upon unemployment. The aim of this article is to put into simple language the prorisions of the Act under the following heads: (a) To whom does the Act apply? (b) What does the Government do? (c) The position of the employer. (d) What has the workman to do? (e) What arc the benefits the workman derives from the Act? (f) How is the Act to be admiristered? (a) The Act applies to 2,500,000 workmen in the following trades: Building, construction of works, shipbuilding, mechanical engineer- ing, ironfounding, construction of vehicles, sawmilling, while in each trade are reckoned all its various branches,

_ . (b) Parliament will contribute to the unem- ployment fund a sum of money equal to one- third of the total contributions of employers and workmen, calculated to amount to £750,000 per annum. Again, the Treasury may advance a sum up to but not exceeding £3,000,000 to meet exceptional claims upon the fund. BY a special order the Board of Trade may extend the Act to workmen in other than insured trades, provided the Gov- ernment contribution for the" three following years does not exceed £1,400,000 per annum. (e) THE POSITION OF THE EMPLOYER.—The sums required for unemployment benefit are to be drawn partly from the employer, who must pay his own and his workmen's contri- butions in the first instance, and may deduct the workmen's contribution from wages. The suns so paid for every workman is fixed at 2id. per week, a broken week to be counted as a whole week, unless the period of un- employment is two (lays or fewer. If the period does not exceed one day, the amount to be paid by employer and workman alike is Id.; if it exceeds one day, 2d. To Stead,/ employment and deca,sualiee labour, one-ihird of the money paid by the employer may be refunded in respect of any workman who has been continuously in his employ for twelve months, and for whom not less than forty-five contributions have been made. (d) What the workman has to do.—Every workman in an insured trade pays for every reek he is employed the suns of 21d., and only while he is employed. Between the ages of seventeen and eighteen the workman pays Id. per week, and is entitled to half benefits. Below the age of seventeen the Act does not apply. To obtain the benefits he must prove: (1) That he has been employed as a work- man in an insured trade in each of not less than twenty-six separate weeks during the preceding five years. (2) That he has made application for benefit in the prescribed manner, and that since the date of application he has bees continuously unemployed. (3) That though capable of working, he is unable to secure employment. (4) That he has not exhausted his right to benefits. (5) That be is not in receipt of eickness or disablement benefits under Part I. No benefits will be paid until after twenty- six weeks' contributions have been paid. A workman cannot claim the benefits if his loss of employment has been occasioned by a trade dispute in the factory where he is em- ployed, by misconduct, or through his having left his employment without just cause—but if he is unemployed by reason of a trade dis- pute elsewhere he can obtain unemployment benefits. _ _

On the other hand, he does not forfeit his claim by declining a situation vacant owing to a trade dispute, nor need .he accept in his own district a wage lower than that to which he has been habitually accustomed, or in other districts, less than the trade union rats of wages. This clause safeguards the current trade union rate of wages. (e) The benefits. In each week succeeding the first week of unemployment, the subscriber receives 75., or such other sum, but the Board of Trade is prohibited from increasing the sum above Sc., or reducing it below 6s. Speaking generally, benefit will not be paid more than fifteen weeks in any one year, and for no period of employment less than one day. A workman cannot receive more benefit than in the proportion of one week's benefit for every five contributions paid; but workmen over the age of twenty-one who have habitually worked at an insured trade before the com- mencement of the Act, will have added to the number of their contributions five extra con- tributions for each period of three months they have worked before the Act commences. The maximum number of contributions thus added by the State will be twenty-five. Arrangements have also been made to suit the cases of those workmen whose wages are paid at longer intervals than a week. But this National Insurance against Unem- ployment becomes in numerous instances a real insurance as well. A workman who has paid 500 contributions, and reached the age of sixty, or later at death, if he has not re- ceived in benefits the total amount of his contributions, shall receive the difference, with interest, between his contributions and the benefits received. _ _ _

If a workman in an insured trade fails to secure employment through some defect of skill or knowledge, the insurance officer is empowered to provide technical instruction out of the unemployment fund. (f) The Act will be administered by the Board of Trade, which will arrange for the payment and collection of contributions by means of stamps on books or cards. The In- surance officers will determine all claims for benefit; but if the workman is dissatisfied he can appeal to the Court of Referees. Ap- peals from the Court of Referees will be decided by an umpire appointed by the King, end his decision is final. When associations tal workmen provide un- employed benefit, the Board of Tra-de, instead of paying the benefit to individual members, can repay to the association the sum which the member would have received in benefits, but not exceeding three-fourths of the amount paid by the -association. Space forbids an exhaustive survey of the Act. Time alone can justify its incep- tion; but before long the nation will re- gard with amazement the humiliating fact that in o, so-called 'civilised era the country was without some form of unemployment in- surance. The Act cannot abolish unemploy- ment, but it can and will alleviate it worst evils, and afford many workmen a certain sense of security which they have never pre- riously enjoyed. The Act comes into force on July 15th, 1912.

NOSITAN FULLET. From the "Feathered World."
LANGSIIANS.

In Langnhans we have two varieties : Croads and Moderns. There is only one colour in Croads (black) while in Moderns there are black, Luff, and blue. Some explanation cf the two varieties is perhaps needed. The word modern as used here does not exactly express the correct meaning of the word because the Modern Langshan, like the Modern Game, have been bred long enough to be called ancient. Therefore, you see at once the word is only used as a distinction between the two varieties.l do not purpose dealing with the merits and demerits of the Moderns at this juncture. The illustration is that of a Croad Langshan pullet, so we must content out selves with a few notes on the Croads.

div.head: CUOAD LANGSHAN
div.p: CUOAD LANGSHAN

As a utility fowl they rank in the very first front. They are essentially an allround breed ; for not only are they well adapted for the farmer but also the town dweller; chiefly because they stand confine- ment well. acd because their dark plumage does not easily show the dirt. If they are m ted for one thing more than another it is for their rich coloured eggs. Scme people are very partial to brown shelled eggs. These ale the fowls above all others that lay them. As a table bird they are excellent and what they lose in dark coloured legs they undoubtedly gain in nice white coloured flesh and of very fine quality. During the past ten years Croad Langshans have regained some of their lost popularity. Now their good qualities are more widely known they will long remain one of our most popular fowl. They are a breed that one feels can be unhesitatingly recommended.

TIMELY HINTS. Now is the time for whitewashing and tarring. You should select a dry windy day for this part of the work. First of all the hen-houses should be thoroughly dismantled of nest boxes and perches. Then give the sides and roof a thorough brush down before applying the lime wash, Before using this however, you should add about one pint of paraffin oil. It is a good insecticide and after an application of limewash so mixed no insect can possibly live. The lime washing should be done in the early part of the day so that it is quite dry before the fowls go to roost. The same night you should examine every individual fowl. If any vermin is foune] give the affected ones a good dusting with Keating's powder. ThAn you can feel quite sure that you have not only ridded the fowl houses of insects but the stock also. A few days after this process take a careful ncte of the habits in the stock. You will find as a result of this cleansing process, they will thrive much better. Being more contented they will give far better returns. One of the first causes for failure in poultrydom is neglect. Some peo2le seem to think that fowls need no assistance. Fowls under natural conditions certainly do not; but under artificial condi- tions fowls cannot get all they require unless their natural habits are studied and their wants accordingly supplied.

THE VALUE OF A PEST OATH. Just as the duck seeks water so does the fowl repair to the hedgerow for a bath. This is the only natural method a fowl has of cleansing its body. Yet how many neglect to supply a substitute. I sat the other day and watched my little pen of Silkies wallowing almost over-head in dust to their greatest satisfaction. It is an easy matter to supply a duet bath. In fine weather you could make a dust bath in the open pen. Dig a good big hole and fill it with di y fine s' il and sand or very fine ashes And for wet weather place a good sized shallow box in the scratch- ing pen and fill it with similar material. The dust bath is a very important item and you will be well repaid for the little extra work entailed in supplying one.

div.head: TIIE CHICKENS.
div.p: TIIE CHICKENS.

I suppose you have all got a brood or two of chicks ere this? Give them your best attention. See that the coops are moved about on to fresh ground every day. Nothing is more detrimental to the health of the yc ung stock than sour and tainted ground. Given proper food and a run on fresh ground you will not be troubled with much sickness amongst the chicks. Change the water vessel as often as convenient but do not place it in the sun. A little flesh meat in some form should be given about every two days. If ycu cannot get cut green bone, give them an occasional feed of bullock's liver, boiled and chopped fine. A little sulphate of iron in the drinking water will serve as a splendid tonic and it will assist them in feather growth wonderfully. If your stock of chickens is not a large one give them an occasional feed of British Bird seed. It is rather too expensive to feed a large stock on this diet, but when it can be given it is a good food. Of course it is a natural diet and its claims will therefore be obvious.

FOWLS IN CONFINEMENT. It is a most difficult matter to keep small fowls such as Bantams and Silkies in laying conditions when kept in close confinement ; and often enough when they do lay you get a large percentage of ehelless eggs. I have recently experi- mented with a trio of Japanese Silkies in this direction. These little fowls are of so contented a nature that they soon become overfat. Consequently when they do lay the eggs are either without shells, or with shells that are very thin. And!.when wanted for sitting purposes they are useless. So I set to work to remedy this difficulty as follows. They were kept in a run about three yards by one yard wide. You will observe jhey had not overmuch room for exercise, thus the difficulty. They had been fed principally on house scraps and wheat. Five out of every eix eggs were unfit for sitting. The shells were so thin that when taken from the nest they cracked with ordinary handling.

CIIINOED TILE DIET. First of all I changed the diet, dropping the wheat altogether and substitute 4 for it bind seed. I con- tinued feeding with a light breakfast of bread and milk ; bitd seed in the evening and green food (a grass sod) at noon. In three weeks tirne under the changed diet they were laying good sound shelled eggs and are now in very good laying condition. This experiment can be applied with larger stock and pro- vided you do not actually starve the fowls you are bound to get good results. There is just as 'much danger in overfeeding fowls as undelfeeding them. Try and remember that under natural conditions a fowl does not get thiee full meals per day. On the other hand they have to work and search for every grain and it stands to reason that where fowls are kept in close confinement they need very special treatment in proper feeding.

div.head: HOWLEY A V. TOWN HALL A.
div.p: HOWLEY A V. TOWN HALL A.

The Town Hall team are now safely in the third round for they beat Howley A by 52 points only three of their men losivg. There was a large amount of interest centred op the game betweed Patrick (Town Hall) and Gleeson (Howley) which resulted in a win for the former by 13-12 after a most exciting game. Patrick gained the lead at the eleventh end and this he main- tained until the 17th end when Gleason led by 12-11. However Patrick got two lovely woods in and won by the odd chalk. There were some fine wins for the Town Hall team and several players on the Howley side did not score more thin half a dozen. Town Hall A, 135, Howley A., 83.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S B V. FAIRFIET,D A.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S B V. FAIRFIET,D A.

This match was undoubtedly the most interesting of the afternoon for St John's only won by eight points. Some keen games were witnessed the most notable of which was the one in which Newts (St John's) lost to Seed by three points, The game was 10-11 at the 14th end but Seed got two goods woods in on the next length and won by 13-10. Tze other games were decided in favour of each team almost alternately and the St John's team have just scrapod in the third round. St John's B 113, Fairfield A 105.
Mr. A. 11. Peacock has promised to visit the Bank Quay grEen on June Ist, when the third round of the Competition will be commenced.
The Liberal Association have joined the British Crown Green Association, and may run a team next season.
LANCASHIRE COUNTY CUP.

After defeating the cup-holders at A igan a week ago great things were expected of the Rylands team on Saturday in the Lancashire County Cup Championship Competition. Their opponents were White&ld and the match was played on the green of Leigh Limited. Excellent weather prevailed and some good bowling was witnessed The fact that the White&ld team only won by 25 points shows that there was little to choose between the teams but still the fact remains and War- rington bas now only two representative teams in the competition. The Rylands men fought hard and the only great Whitefield victory Tilts the one in which T Wardle beat H Shaw by 21-4. The locals teemed to have had no luck for most of the men only lost by three and two points. W Roughly (Rylands) played a good game and beat R Eastwood by 2 l-11. H Eyes, A Stringer and W Daniels all of Rylands were successful in beating their opponents R Rothwell, E Nuttall and H Allen by three, seven and two points respectively. The final scores were Whitefleld 230, Rylands Reca 205.

div.head: SECOND TEAMS.
div.p: SECOND TEAMS.

At the Nag's Head, Urmston. on Saturday the Rylands' 2ad team mct Radcliffe Withinsand after some very exciting games, lost by a score oi points, H Roughley (Etylanda) did not quite come up to his usual standard and lost to F Rigby by 4-21. However the other men were in capital form and made a plucky stand og tinst:their opponents. Some tight games were decided on either side and although beaten, the Rylands team were in no way disgraced. The totals were :—Radcliff a Withins 227, Rylands 207.

There are still two Warrington teams in the competi- tion, Cemetery and Whitecross, It was rather unfortu- nate that Warrington Cemetery should have been drawn with the local Bull's Head team, for in that Case we we e bound to have one less local team in the fourth round. The CemEtery team won at Liverpool over their opponents who were cup holders in 1908. On the ground at Newton, Whitecross beat Leigh Limited, and Warrington's hopes in this competition must now rest with these two teams who have some capital men and should fight bard for honours.

div.head: CRICKET NOTES.
div.p: CRICKET NOTES.

Warrington are still waiting to record their first victory of the season. On Saturday they encountered formidable foes at Stockport and did well to avert disaster, for the home eleven had much the better of the batting and, wicket for wicket, undoubtedly carried off the honours. Actually, the result was of the kind to which the Warrington supporters are becoming most accustomed—a draw—but it is within the bounds of possibility that, had time their
• • allowed, the visitors would have _ reached

opponents total before their 1,...5t wicket fell. On an equality of wickets—five—they were 50 in arrears. Stockport took first turn with the bat and with the advent of J S Cragg it speedily became evident that their position was secure.He was at the top of his form and gave the bowlers a warm time, changes being tried without avail. However, when his total had reached 120 he played one of Silcock's deliveries into the hands of Wright. Cragg was far and away the most successful batsman of the afternoon. Next on the home eleven came S. R. N. Stockdale who smartly compiled 41. before Hodgson bowled him. 13. Silcock and W. Bennett came out with the best bowling achievements, taking two wickets for 16 runs and two wickets for 35 runs respectively. The home innings was declared at 209 for five wickets.

The Warringtonians set to work manfully, and although their innings presented nothing of dazzling brilliance, several of the batsmen gave very sound displays. F. Callon did exceptionally well for his 41, and we had also refreshing cricket from W. Richard- son and T. Wright, who played 37 and 31 respectively to their credit. J. W. Pearson had got well set when stumps were drawn, and carried out his bat with 25 to his account. . _

Warrington 2nd experienced an uncommonly bad time at the hands of Stockport 2nd, who went about their work in the most thorough-going fashion and piled on the comfortable little margin of 213 with a wicket to spare. The home batsmen, for the most part, were in wretched form and were all tumbled out for 68. The only players to obtain double figures were J Bainbridge (22) and 11 Dolan (20). The visitors had matters all their own way, the chief feature of their innings being a great display by J Lister, who put together 129. They ceased at 281 for nine wickets.

The Warrington and District League tourney yielded a surprise in the shape of a remarkably keen tight between the Conservatives and Whitecross. The champions libel all their work cut out to win, in fact they only succeeded in retaining their unbeaten certificate by a single run. For the Conservatives W Hunter was in tine form with the willow and compiled 16. W W Hill (11) made the best effort for the wire- men. Green bowled very effectively for the winners, while Barrow put in some fine work with the ball for Whitecross.
Wilderspool and Orford were also pretty evenly matched, the villagers triumphing by tbreo runs. The scoring all round as low, but only oce player—Clarke (10—getting more than 10. •

Sankey inflicted a heavy reverse on Walker's Brewery, the respective scores being 109 and 50. The mainstay of the victors in the batting department was Forster, who secured the capital total of 43 by excelled batting. Daintith was run out for 12.
To-day's fixtures are : St Helens Cable v Walker's. Whitecross v Orford. Warrington Conservatives v IVilderspool. Cairo-street v Sankey.

-- The match between Workingmen's Mission and Brick- street, in the Warrington and District Sunday School League, was of a farcial character. Brick-street must be badly in need of practice, for with the solitary exception of B Pridden—who made 4—each of their men came out with a "duck." "Mr Extra" obligingly added 3. Total of innings, 7. Workingmen's Mission had not much to do to beat this, and their score came to 53, E Spruce being the top batsman with 11.

An official of the Workingmen's Mission Club, writes to point out that the mach between Vgorkingmen's Mission and Orford St. John's last week did not result in a draw, as reported, the Mission being beaten by 51 runs to 4. Some confusion has apparently arisen as to hwho wss said to have been "note i g si innings ." s of fact, writes our corres- er the of H a Corlett,m s pondent, Corlett was "run Out" according to the umpire's decision which must be final. When ths decision was made there were many different opinions expressed on the matter. Even the umpires disagreed, but the umpire at the batter's end gave "out" and therefore his decision must bold good.
The Sunday School League matches for to-day are:— Bold-street v Workingmen's Miasion. Stockton Heath v Orford St. John's, Brick-street v Walton Choir.
Ryland's Recreation had no difficulty in disposing of St. Paul's, G. Gough with 19 being the best individual score. G. McGowan captured eight wickets for 13 runs.

Emmanuel Institute tried conclusions with Liver- pool Farm School (Newton) but suffered defeat after a good fight. Roebuck was in brilliant form for the home team, making 54 not out, while S. Oakes captured four wickets for 13 runs.

Warrington Cable Works came a cropper at Helsby, the villagers obtaining a majority of 27. A Cartwright (25) made the top score of the match and J H C Brooking (15) was the most successful batsman for the Cable Works.
Latchford Baptists inflicted a crushing defeat on Winwick Asylum. thanks largely to the excellent batting of J Cox (39), R Gibson (29) and J Ashton (17). For Winwick Brunton batted well for 22.
Lymm visited South West Manchester and were victorious by 16. There was nothing very noticeable about the match, R Bell being the winners' top scorer with 11.

Grappenball failed to account for Altrincham who put together 61 against their 53. Neither contingent did anything great in the way of batting, A Turner who made 14 for the winners, making the best performance. A Hutchings knocked up 12 for Grappenhall.

Golborne-street Baptists were beaten by Bank-street Mission—a promising team which knocked up GO runs as compared with the Baptists' 37, II Knight, 15, batted well for the visitors, while T Woodhead compiled 20 and took three wickets for 13 runs for the Baptists. 0 Woodhead took six wickets for 30 runs.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
Local Successes.

On Saturday last at Leigh Harriers' Sports members of Warrington Athletic Club annexed three first prizes. In the 100 yards handicap Harold Povey, with 10 yards start, won his heat, second round, and final in 10 seconds, or a shade inside, and had a good two yards advantage over his nearest opponent. From the 18 yards mark Povey won the lastest heat of the 220 yards handicap in 22 3-5 seconds, and with 6 yards to spare won the final in 22 2-5 seconds. Povey is a native of Orford village, and as he is only 21 years old should gain further prizes. A sitting-room suite end a hand- some case of cutlery rewarded his latest efforts. His previous successes were first in the 220 yards at Warrington Charities Sports, and third in 220 yards at Cheshire Lines Sports in 1910. Another resident of Orford, Chris Vose, now has a massive oak 8-day semi-grandfather's clock to com- memorate a fine piece of running in the two-mile race which, less 185 yards, Vose covered in 9 min. 29 secs., and he has apparently quite recovered from the illness which prevented him maintaining his title of Northern Cross Country Champion. Vose has paid little attention to track running since he won the one mile handicap on the same ground in 1910; he is undoubtedly one of the best cross country men and his form "For England" in the last two international races should merit his selection for the Olympic games at Stockholm. John Henry Ardern, of High Leigh, joined \Carring- ton Athletic Club, last season and opened his prize list by winning their half mile cycle handicap, then he got a second at Bollington, first at Tideswell, and first at Doncaster, all in half mile cycle handicaps on grass. On Saturday last he brought away from %Vest Cheshire Harriers Sports at Ellesmere Port, a marble clock and ornaments, also a silver set of sugar basin, cream jug and spoons, as mementos of ready victories in the half mile and one mile handicaps.

div.head: LANCASHIRE AMATEUR ASSOCIATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE AMATEUR ASSOCIATION.

Further progress was made in the Lancashire Cup and County Championship on Saturday, when the 16 surviv- ing clubs met in the third round of the Cup competition in Lancashire. At Liverpool two ex-holders of the Cup were in opposition—the rival Warrington teams meet- ing from the Bull's Head and Cemetery Hotels, whilst Leigh Railway (five times winners of the Cup) and Roebuck Hotel (champions 1910) visited Irlam and Swinton respectively. Nay was also resumed in the Lanctv.hire Association Championship Consolation for teams defeated in the first round of the Cup, whilst the Second Teams Championship second round was also decided. The " tit-bit " of the draw was the meeting of the holders, Whitefield, and Griffin Hotel at Harpurhey. Whitefield have on six occasions carried off the championship. Parliament has risen PARLIAMENT for the Whitsuntide AND THE holidays, and Tuesday TITANIC in the House of Commons was what may be called one of the settling-up days. As the affairs of the Board of Trade came before the House it became possible to discuss the position of that Department in relation to the Titanic disaster, and some of the speeches on the subject showed in a I striking manner how very practical a body the House Of Commons can be on the proper occasion. There are specialists on one subject or another on all the benches, and on each side of the House, and certainly the shipping industry is never without power- ful representatives when any subject which touches it, nearly comes before Parliament. Speeches made both from the Ministerial and the Opposition benches are deserving of much public attention. The attempt to place the blame of the Titanic disaster on the Board of Trade has been somewhat of a party character, but we are not disposed to suggest that Tuesday's discussion had a party origin, though it was initiated by a Conservative member. MAJOR ARCHER SHEE blamed the Department in severe terms, mainly on the ground that it has permitted clearly obsolete regulations to remain in force until it has been awakened by an unparalleled disaster. The truth is, of course, that the Board of Trade has been inquiring for some years past into the very matter that has now become urgent, and that it had new proposals before it at the time of the Titanic disaster. Probably it has dawdled. All Government departments dawdle. However strenuous Ministers may be they find the barnacles in the way.

It did not at all appear from the discussion, however, that the obsoleteness of the regulations of the Board of Trade were in any way responsible for the great lass of life on the Titanic. Very experienced shipowners, and even LORD CHARLES BERESFORD, are clearly of opinion that the provision of a greater number of boats would not be likely to result in a larger saving of life if the weather were such as that in which shipwrecks ordinarily take place. We do I not suggest, however, that this exonerates the Board of Trade, or, for that matter, the owners of hugh passenger ships. The question of life-saving under the new con- ditions which have arisen out of the construction of vast ocean liners is obviously one for immediate consideration. The theory of unsinkableness is something that is disposed of for ever.

MR TYRRELL, who spoke from an intimate knowledge of seafaring matters, thinks th the Board of Trade is overweighted, and he is probably right. It has been relieved of a portion of its duties during the last few years. The Fisheries Department has been passed over to the Board of Agriculture; but there might reasonably be some more un- loading. The present suggestion is that there should be a subordinate department of the Board to deal specially with merchant shipping. This would be a development rather than a new departure; and we may assume from what was said on Tuesday that it would satisfy both MR TYRRE LL and LORD CHARLES BERESFORD. MR 1-JOLT, the member for the Hexham Division of Northumberland, who is a Liverpool ship- owner, contributed to the debate a speech of an exceedingly useful character, which was to some extent a defence of the Government department which was attacked. In his opinion the cry for more boats is a delusion and a snare. However great was the number of boats, could they be launched? That was one of the important questions which he raised. Whereas boats on ocean liners had to be lowered only about 25 feet in days comparatively recent, they have now to be lowered 70 feet or so, with the practical certainty that in stormy weather they will be rendered useless before they can reach the surface of the sea.

Clearly there are many points of view from which the loss of the Titanic must be investigated. But there are not more than two points on which it is judicious to be positive at the present stage. One is that when ice is known to be at hand the course of a vessel should be so changed as to avoid it. The other is that when a great vessel finds itself in a field of ice it should not go full steam ahead.

Mr. Herbert Samuel POST OFFICE had not only a striking REFORMS, record of success to lay before the House in respect of Post Office administration, but a striking series of reforms to announce. The Empire is to be linked up with a wireless telegraphic service. An underground rail- way system has been planned for the carriage of mails through London. On the one hand this is a boon to Londoners, who will obtain, not only a quicker delivery,but relief from the nocturnal disturbances by heavy mail vans which have murdered sleep. On the other hand, there are few districts of Great Britain the inhabitants of which will not gain to some extent by "quicker mail transit in the great postal and business clearing-house of the Empire. Night telegrams at reduced rates and the development of telephonic communication with the Continent may also be singled out from a host of reforms,effected or in process.
The Progressive Labour

SUMMER League is to be con- CAMPAIGN OPENS. gratulated upon the auspicious opening of its summer campaign. In attendance, enthusiasm, and the quality of the speeches the great open-air meeting on Monday even- ing ranked worthily with the splendid series for which the League has been responsible in the course of its long and strenuous educa- tional propaganda. Mr. Jeremiah MacVeagh, •M.P„ is one of the most brilliant and per- suasive advocates of the cause of self- government for Ireland, and his speech not only presented an unanswerable array of arguments,but sparkled withw it and humour. His crisp criticisms of the brothers Smith were especially apropos, and he made short work of "F. E.'s " tall talk about revolution in Ulster. The feature of the speech which should command close attention was the case for Home Rule from the British and Imperial standpoint, Mr McVeagh showing that it would conduce to the more efficient working of the Parliamentary machine and an adequate consideration of topics which at present must of necessity receive perfunctory treatment. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who had, as usual, a very cordial greeting, devoted a large part of his interesting speech to the Irish question, but also touched in cogent and forceful style upon some pressing industrial and social problems, incidentally , dealing with the discreditable tactics of the Tories with regard to the Insurance Act.
The Education Corn-
LOCAL mittee, on Monday HEADMASTERSHIPS. evening, had a full

dress -debate on the vexed question of appointments to local head- masterships. Mr. Upson tested the feeling of the Committee by moving a resolution : "That all appointments to the headships of elementary Council schools shall, in future, be made from the teachers in the enploy of the Committee." After a discussion which thoroughly ventilated the question the Com- mittee rejected the resolution by 14 votes to 5. Without being in any way inconsistent, we think we may give the Committee credit for:coming to a wise decision. Mr.Upson was probably little disappointed i with the fate of his motion—it was not at all likely that the Committee would tie its hands so deliberately and firmly in regard to all future appointments. A good deal can be said, and was said, on behalf of the resolution but it must be conceded that the best educational interests would not be served by eliminating open competition for headmasterships. The teachers—smarting under a real grievance as they are—would probably admit so much. What seems to us to be necessary is for the Education Com- mittee to realise that open competition is not an absolute essential in every case. A hard and fast rule is just as objectionable one way as the other, and we hold to our opinion that the Evelyn-street appointment is a case in point. This headmastership could have been allotted to a local applicant with more cer- tainty of the best results than was obtained by the method which aroused so much opposition. The Committee owes a fuller and more tangible preference to its own teachers than has heretofore been manifested. That is all !
It is one of the fa vour- A FLIPPANT ite assumptions of the ASSUMPTION. Tariff Reform party

that a measure of Free Trade between Canada and the United States would lead to the loss of the British Colony. That is how they interpret the observation of President Taft to the effect that if there were a lower tariff wall between those two adjacent countries Canada would become an " adjunct " of the United States. Not only is there no foundation for such an assump- tion, but when it is laid out and looked at the argument recoils upon the Tariff Reformers themselves. For these Tariff Reformers are the same people who would put an end to the Free Trade we give Canada. If Free Trade in North America makes for annexation, Protection in the British Empire must make for separation. Shall we shut out Canadian commerce as America prepares to let it in? There is no Tariff wall raised in this country against Canada. She remains loyal. But should the Tariff wall now standing against her in the United States be pulled down,then Canala, we are asked to suppose, would turn her back on the Mother Country, and trans- fer her loyalty to her nearest neighbour.That is the " argument " over here. And a pretty piece of Protectionist flippancy it is !
A letter in the Times A REMARKABLE which has attracted LETTER. much attention was

contributed by Sir Morgan O'Connell, a Unionist landlord. Sir Morgan O'Connell declares that he was opposed to Home Rule because he read it as "Separation." But "the most strenuous opponent" of the Home Rule Bill cannot say that it is separation. The Lords, he assumes, will throw out any Bill that can be called Home Rule. But, if a General Election takes place, and the Unionist Party is returned to power, "can they hope to have and keep such a majority as will enable them to look upon the votes of eighty-one Nationalist Members as of no account ?" Mr. Bonar Law has promised Tariff Reform and extended land purchase as an alternative to Home Rule. Fifty millions of money spent in land purchase have not turned a single district councillor, outside Ulster, against Home Rule. What would it cost to make eighty-one Nationalist Members, by the process of " killing Home Rule with kindness," into Unionists? Sir Morgan O'Connell concludes that there are only two ways of dealing with the Irish problem : (1) To give Ireland the right to manage her own local affairs, and convert her from a danger into a factor of strength in the Empire; (2) To disfranchise every Nationalist con- stituency. Even Sir Edward Carson would shrink from the horn of this dilemma.

div.head: DEATH OF MR: JOHN HENRY MOUNFIELD. '
div.p: DEATH OF MR: JOHN HENRY MOUNFIELD. '

We regret to record the death of Mr. John H. Mounfield,of Walton-road, Stockton Beath, who passed away suddenly at 6.30 last evening. He had been in depressed health daring the past two years, but the end came unexpectedly and was due to heart failure. Mr. Mounfield was the fourth son of the late Joseph Mounfield, well known as a cabinet maker, 9, Butter- market-street. He received a training in the business and for many years took a leading share in the man- agement of the firm of Joseph Mounfield and Sons. He was well known and widely respected in that capacity, and his retiremeat a year or two ago gave great regret to many with whom he had been associated in business. He leaves a widow, two sons and three daughters.

div.head: LPl.xami-ner, Saturday, May, 25, 1912. WARSHIPS IN THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: The LPl.xami-ner, Saturday, May, 25, 1912. WARSHIPS IN THE SHIP CANAL.
Photo Drury. Stockton Heath. THE CRUISER " BRISTOL " PASSING THROUGH STOCKTON HEATH AT 4.30 P.M. YESTERDAY.

The passage up the Ship Canal yesterday of the fine cruiser Bristol, and the four destroyers Zulu, Amazon, Nubian, and Hope, en route to Manchester Docks,"aroused grcat interest all along the waterway, and crowds lined the banks almost without a break. It is eleven years since warships previously caine up the canal, and then we had on:y the pleasure of receiving destroyers. For a prior visit of a cruiser we have to go back to the opening of the canal by Queen Victoria on May 21st, 1894.

The four destroyers were soon on the way—and up to schedule time—a start being made from Eastham about 6 a.m. By B.3othe squat, black and grim-looking "speed merchants" of the Navy were at Latchford, ready for the passage through the locks. A large number of people assembled at the three local swing-bridges, and raised a hearty cheer for the strange visitors. Every one was responded to in lusty fashion by the jack-tars who manned the circumscribed decks of the destroyers. Everybody was, however, agog to see the fine cruiser Bristol, 4,800 tons, 4301 t. long, 24,529 h.p., and speed. 2684 knots. She carries two 6in. guns, two torpedo tubes, and a crew of 376. Unfortunately she was nowhere to be seen in the rear of the destroyers, and hours elapsed before definite news arrived that her masts were too high to pass under Runcorn Bridge. Considerable delay• occurred before the masts were short- ened, and it was 4.30 in the afternoon before the graceful but formidable craft sailed past the borders of old Warrington.
