MR. H. MORISON (L.) who yesterday won for the Libarals the seat vacated by Mr. Bottomley. The poll was: Morison Gibson. Majority 703 • PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There are features of special interest in the bill at the Hippodrome this week, though the programme is exceptionally good throughout. Jack Sheridan, son of the famous Mark Sheridan, is "following in father's footsteps "and his debut before a Wartington audi- ence was immensely successful on Monday evening. I He has a lot of the Sheridan mannerisms and stock- I in-trade, but is no mere copyist. Young Sheridan has humour of his own, a style which " takes " and plenty of confidence. He had his audience in roars of laughter most of the time. One of the best sketches seen in Friars' Green for some time is " Mortimer Magnus, M.P.," introducing that marvel of juvenile precocity, Master Edward Garrett in the title role. The youngster's first appearance is effective and unexpected from a kit-bag of quite modest dimensions He emerges with tall hat, frcck coat, etc., And looks the typical M.P., on business bent. He and his secretary have apparently sought refuge from the suffragettes in a High School, where the minute Mortimer is taken for a "new boy " by the Lady Piincipal and goes through some screamingly funny adventures. Master Garrett is exceedingly I droll, and a good word should be said for Miss Montrose, who !represents to perfection the school mistress of fiction. As a change from the laughter- makers we have also some very smart dancing by a youthful trio known as The Three Its, one of whom is a twelve year old wonder. Ida Revell, the "versatile chorus comedienne" has methods of her own. She is not great as a vocalist, but she makes the chorus " go " and scores a success where least expected. John Donald presents his moving song scena Scottish Exile's Dream" with mach effect, and Lilian Gould sings " Shadows " in excellent voice and style. Ulrick performs wonders in the way of balancing a barrel on his feet, and the three Laseelles conclude the enter- tainment with a comedy act " The Aviators," which is good, but capable of improvement. A few of the jokes are much older than aviation, whereas they should certainly be airy trifles.

Next week a good bill is headed by Signor Arvi, Italian illusionist who will present the great Arvi mystery comprising music science, art and of course mystery. Alan Borthwaite and Cc, will appear in the sketch "Half-a-dollar." The Croisit trio, acrobatic act; the Sisters Storm, vccalists and dancers ; Alf Brookes, comedian and others will also appear.

div.head: WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION. Conference at Warrington. FIGHTING THE DRINK EVIL.
div.p: WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION. Conference at Warrington. FIGHTING THE DRINK EVIL.

The British VC7ornen's Temperance Association still continues its on card march and as each year passes by we are made more billy aware of the good work this society is doing and a hat it is intetded to do in the future to stamp out the evils due to drink. One of tbe most promicent branches in this organisation is tbe Warrington branch which boasts a membership of 500 and has accomplished much useful propaganda work in the town. On Wednesday afternoon a County Union Conference was held in the Bold-street Schoolroom and a large number of delegates attended. Miss Bertha Mason an official of the association presided and on taking the chair she received a beautiful bunch of flowers from the hands of Mrs. Owen, the vice- president of the Warrington Branch, on behalf of the members. Miss Mason spoke on the National Insur- ance Act and begged the members to insure in approved temperance societies. She also dealt with whet had been done at the National Association meeting, which had been held at Newcastle, in regard to the great measure. The benefits which cna woula derive from joining a wholly temperance society, they all well knew, and as there was net much time before the 15th July, she urged them to join as early as possible and thus get the best , possible insurance under the Act. Sabsequently Mrs SHILTON WATKINS conducted a school of method ia which amusing mistakes were made and rectified to show how a model committee should be conduated. Mrs Simpson, lac;n secretary of the War- rington branch, Mrs Watson, lion secretary of the County Union, and Mrs Iligham, treasurer of the County Union, and others took part ie the model committee meeting. In the evening there was a fair attendance in the schoolroom' when a public meetiiig was held. Miss Bessie Dutton presided and she was supported by Miss B Mason, Mrs Simpson, Mrs Watson, Mrs Owen, the Revs H Ogden and J S Chedburn. MISS DUTTON at the outset said she had a great feeling for that noble cause and emphasised the usefulness of uniting together and of organisation. A great deal could be done by joining together, and a great number of fortresses which had been considered impregnable had been taken by united effort. Evils which had been considered inconquerable had been overcome, and the strongholds of vice bad been cap- tured. What a blessed thing it was that the great evil —drink—in our land had been gripped, and although not yet conquered, they were gradually working their way towards its complete subjection. Every year they seemed to recognise some weak point in which they could get a foothold for its destruction. Then there was the individual work. Co-operation was a splendid thine., but she would ask them te ;think of what they could do by their quiet personal influence. They needed courage to he able to carry on the good work, and she was sure they were all proud to belong to such an admirable association. (Applause). Miss BERTHA MASON dealt at some length with the history of the Association and told in a lucid manner how the society Pad been commenced and how it had progressed since 187 G. She also stated amid applause that the membership of the association was I now 155,000, and they were in a wholly solvent position. However, what they had done in the past was only one side of the question, they had an enormous amount of work to do yet before their ambitions could be realised. First of all she wanted to congratulate the Warrington branch on winning the shield, which was on the platform, for having secured the largest number of members in the previous sear. (Applause.) The question now was how to keep those members, and they had not only to keep those but increase their member- ship. They had need of rapid progress. When they considered that the drink bill for a year was £160,000,000 they recognised the enormous amount of work that had to be done, (bear, hear), before they could get that bill lessened and removed from the land. She believed it was a fact that in spite of their efforts, as much alcohol was being con- sumed now as 70 years ago. Prevention was far better than cure, and quick as they had been travelling in the past, the pace of the foe was so fase that they would have to move quicker still. If the country was to be saved from the awful effects of strong drink they realised that they must save the children—(hear,hear)— land the responsibility rested with the men and women of to-day. The children would constitute the nation of to-morrow, and it was they:whom they should help, for it W 39 upon the children that the hope of the future rested. (Hear, hear.) The parents should show the children by precept and example how to become the men and women it was desired they should become. The precepts of the teachers in school were of no avail unless a good example was set the children when they arrived home. (Hear, bear.) The supreme need of the nation to-dayle-a5 good motherhood,because in the hands of mothers the care and trust of the children was lay. The parents could make it difficult for the children to do wrong and easy for them to do right by their precept and example. (Applause). Miss Mason then presented stars of honour to those members who had obtained 12 new members and these were :—The Misses Beatrice Daley, Mary and Jane Lewers and Lizzie Whalley. Two book prizes were presented to Miss M J Robinson and Mrs Simpson who had obtained their second batch of 12 members. A framed pictore was also presented to the Independent Methodists, Grappenball, to be hung in the room where 12 new Members had been secured. The Rev. H. OGDEN, in the course of an address,said that the temperance question was without doubt a
QUE RAIN-SPOUT FROM BUTTERMARKET-STREET.

The above is a ph-itograph of a unique lend spo a- head brought to light during the demolition of property in Bottermarket-street. It was found on the building formetly in the ccoupition of the late Mr. Adam Webster,tailor, and the data-1720 —is believed lobe that of the erection of the structure. The initials N. and T. probably represent the Christian names of the builder of the house and his wife, while W. stands for the surname. Perhaps some reader can explain the significance of the ornamental work, At present this interesting relic of old Warrington reposes in the Museum.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" lha Lifeguardsman."

If all dramas possessed the same excellent qualities as Walter 'Toward's new play "The Lifeguardsman," staged at the Court Theatre this week, the popularity of this class of entertainment, which, owing to inferior productions is fast disappearing, would no doubt be revived and the time would come when the public would take the same interest in plays as a quarter of a century ago. The visit of this thrilling, romantic military play to Warrington has been a successful one and nightly large crowds of people have visited the Rylands-street house and enjoyed to the full the excellent dramatic fare provided. A pleasing feature of the production is that the plot is not one of those painfully intricate ones, but it is simple in all its effectiveness. Practically the whole stoiy is revealed in the first act when the Princess of Rhineland is ordered by her minister to marry within two days for the well-being of tne nation. The wish of her government is that she should marry Prince Hugo of Sax-Steinberg, a personage she utterly distrusts' Whilst on his way to the palace "The Lifeguardsman" meets the princess but is under the impression that she is a maid of honour. The inevitable happens but it is not until he has avowed his devotion that he learns the truth. Thus a keen rivalry is set up between the Lifeguardsman and Hugo and with deep cunning the Prince contrives to keep his rival out of the way until he has apparently won the Princess. However after a very realistic motor race and an accident the lifeguardsrnan wins by" a short head "and eventually secures the hand of his lady-love as the last of the 43 hours is passing, much to the discomfiture of the enraged prince. Possessed of a dignified and charming personality, Miss Beth Elliot plays the part of the princess in a truly royal manner and in her tribula- tion solicits with success the ..sympathy and feeling of the audience. Mr. Fred Emery makes a capital Lifeguardsman and with his brusque military manner he shares equally in the success of his partner. Mr. William Calvert has a difficult role, that of the drunken prince Hugo, but nevertheless be is success- ful in his endeavours to make the part as repulsive as it should be. The humour of the play is in the able hands of Mr. T. G. Vane as Spiff, supported by two fellow lieutenants. Mr. Reginald Fry and Mr. Melville Chiswell as Tosh and Dinkie respectively. Spiff is highly amusing, and his facial expressions and cmtortions in the ghost Beene were well, but not overdone, and indeed in all his eccentricities he proved himself an accomplished actor as well as a successful laughter provoker. Miss Jessica Black played the part of the mad prince in a I clever manner and at once gained the sympathy of the audience. Mr. W. T. Elworthy as the plotting prime minister to the princess, showed that he had real skill and used it to the best advantage in proving an able accomplice to Pi ince Hugo. Mr. Wilfred Grahame gave an impressive portrayal of the part of the kind-hearted General Roseberg and Miss Ruth Dockray as the waiting maidand Miss Nana Flinsberg

as Sylvia, als) add to the humour of the piece. The other parts are in fqually able hands an I the scenic effec's and gorgeous unif )rms lend additioaal effect and add to the SUCCF EIS of the production. NEXT WEEKS PROGRAMME. "THE t:PECKLED BAND." A powerful play will visit Warrington on Monday next in the great Adelphi succes., "The Speckled Band," from the pen rf Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. This piece has vi-ited Manchester "Princes •' and the "Royal" Theatres five times in 18 months so there is no question as to its drawing powers. Competent critics express the opinion that it is one of Conan Doyle's best efforts. It is full of sensation, while it is void of those crudities sometimes seen in the average drama. '[he company is a powerful one including Mr. James C. Taylor as Dr. Itylatt and Mr. Herbert Bradford as Sherlock Holmes, and is under the direction of Mr. Arthur Hardy, who was responsible for the oiiginal produc- tion at the Adelphi Theatre, London, where it ran for over 15 months and was then transferred to the St. James' Theatre, when it was impossible to further delay the producton of " The Quaker Girl." With such an attraction, 1: oil playgoers should attend in largo numbers on Monday, and thus prove their appre- ciation of the management's endeavours to give them of the best.

woman's question because women suffered from the effects of intemperance much more than men. (Hear hear.) Again it was a woman's problem because it directly affected the children. There might be tragedies enacted in many homes in Warrington that night of which they would never hear. Tragedies which would be the result of drink. When they got at the unfortunates, the degraded, bedraggled and shameless, they invariably found that such were the product of the public-house. Continuing the rev, gentleman said that suppose the public-houses were taken away what were they going to institute in their place for the working man ? Unfortunately in many !cases, the only club a poor man had was the public-house, and that was probably the only place where he wo aid be welcomed. He hid noticed in Warrington that in the midst of a poor district the most palatial building was the public- house. If streets were made in Hell they could not be made worse than some of the streets in Bewsey. Bt then the fact remained that a man must have somewhere to go, and if he only got Cl per week and bad a wife and four children he could not live in Stockton Heath. Bewsey and Bewsey only for him ! The social instinct was in every man and if the public-house was taken away they would have to substitute something in its place. (Hear, hear.) He believed in women having the controlling views in each matters, as they knew of the great amount of suffering which generally accompanied the use of strong drink. Continuing, Mr. Ogden said that one of the curves, the greatest curse so far as the drinking trade was concerned, was the vested interest of the Trade." That vested interest laid its huge bands on municipal tintless and laid the same grip and hold rn the National Government. Why could it not be4placed in the hands of disinterested men and out of the profits why should they not erect in such places as Bewsey the winter palace where a man could find in winter the equivalent to whit he had in summer in the parks? If the" Trade" was to continue then the profits should be used for the relief and benefit of society. He was a prohibitionist and believed in local veto and local option but whilst they were destroying they should not forget to build up. (Applause). Mrs. OWEN then gave a temperance reading and Miss MA SON said that they, as British women, were strongly against any scheme whereby the proceeds of drink were devoted for the erection of counter-attractions. Drink was bad no matter whether it was sold by a bishop or a publican. (Hear, hear). The Bev J S CH EDB URN gave an interesting address, in the course of which he said it was women who endured the bitterest suffering and sustained the greatest loss and had to bear the heaviest burdens incidental to the gigantic tyranny. He could in some measure understand men being cool and indifferent about temperance reforra and even hostile to it. Their business interests and what they called their pleasure were so deeply involved, and they were only conscious of a very small proportion of the misery and the woe for which drink was responsible He could not understand how any woman worthy of the name could be indifferent or could help being an ardent and determined and relentless enemy to the accursed traffic. Then there were the interests of the children, which were supremely he responsibility of the women. He rejoiced that in the British Women's Temperance Association they had proof that the women of the realm had awakened to the truth and had massed themselves with all the extra- ordinary powers they possessed in mighty array against their common foe. (Applause). During the evening Miss Eva Tanner delighted the audience with her singing and a hearty vote of thanks to all who had taken part was given.

div.head: CYCLIST'S NOTE-BOOK. [By " Silver Street."]
div.p: THE CYCLIST'S NOTE-BOOK. [By " Silver Street."]

I will finish my remarks about Dolgelly this week to give those who have opportunity and desire the means of seeing a most charming part of Wales. And first is the ride down to Barmouth, ten miles. As you can cross the little river Mawddach by three bridges you have a good choke of routes, either of which is superbly fine. I believe it was Ruskin who was asked which was the finest drive lie had ever enjoyed. Ile said "The finest in Europe is from Dolgelly to Barmouth; and the second is from Barmouth to Dolgelly." Go by train, and half of the view in any case is lost, for you can only look out of one window at a time, and if You happen to have got into a crowded train you are stuck in the middle and can't see any. If a gale is blowing up the estuary the passage of two of the bridges is not the easiest thing. I remember on one occasion crossing that at Penmtunpool when my companion had the greatest difficulty in bolding her bicycle from being blown against the railings, in which case the danger would have been very real. She could not dis- mount either, and it took the strength of both to get across and into safety. Every one knows the Panorama Walk,the Torrent walk,and the Precipice walk from P.P.C.'s, of which the last is by far the most impressive. But all three, together with the climbing of Cader Idris, are not for cyclists, and so we will take the sights worth noting for our cycle runs. By taking the road above the stream that gives the name to the Torrent Walk, as far as the Cross Foxes Inn, and then turning to the right the torn up road is soon passed and the top reached, and a magnificent coast commences. The first little lake on the left is the Three Pebble Pool, Llyn Trigraienyn. You can see the three pebbles by the side of the lake, and that is the proof of the story of how Idris the giant felt uncomfortable as he strode from Cader Ito the hill on the left and shook these bits of stone 1(40 or 50 tons each) out of his shoe. Of course the whole district is associated with such fables, which you can find in one guide book or another. But our journey takes us on to the next lake, Talyllyn The first inn, the Tynycornel is as good as the other. and more reasonable, I think. tt the next village, Abergynolwyn a turn is taken to the right, and at Llanegryn (6 miles) the way may be asked to Tonvanna station--that is not the way the Welsh spell it. Leaving the cycle at the station make your way to the shore, where you can make a collection of sea shells such as you don't find everywhere on our coast. Dog whelks, bivavles of many kinds, and not least a beautiful species of cowrie, the only one I have seen on the British coasts. The return to Dolgelly is by way of Arthog. Another and better shell beach is at Llanbedr via 13armouth. If you choose a time when the tide is low you can wade across to the island or bank of Mochras (shell island), or by leaving cycles at Llanbedr station a fisherman will row you across (9d. each we paid). In some places by skimming the top of the bank, nothing but lovely minute shells are gathered. They seem, like the Tonvanna shells, to be bred on the long bank, stretch- ing out into Cardigan Bay for 14 miles, and washed up by the storms. Sometimes they are exceedingly plentiful, sometimes nearly disappear. But if you have children of your own or of somebody else, to whom you want to give hours of delight, don't forget to send home a bag of jetsam from Llanbedr. One more charming round before I have done with Dolgelly. Over by the Cross Foxes again, and down the Talyllyn pass until you are about a mile from the lake. Then turn left to the Corns Valley. At one time busy as Dinorwic or BE thesda with the slate trade this valley is now nearly silent. But the little toy railway that keeps company with our road the whole way down the valley is a marvel to a Warringtonian. One ot the regulations you may read in any of the (ahem !) stations, is that the booking office must close five minutes before the time the train ought to come in. Afraid of the crush, I dare- say. Another is that "although the company start at the advertised time, they shall not go off before that time." So all aboard that are going aboard S:c ! The Corns Valley is loveliness itself, and the road is a capital S. At the bottom is Mdclunlleth, a market town that is like most other such Welsh towns, but our road lies along the near side of the valley, for we must see that sweetest of all Welsh seaside places, Aberdovey. Everything about Aberdovey is delightful, the bids, the estuary, the quaint old stone quays; and the seven miles of road which keeps such close company with the Cambrian railway are by no means spoiled by the nearness of the little single line. Turning northward from Aberdovey we reach Towyn and are soon on our old road through LI wyngwril and Arthog. The whole of to-day's round is 47 miles, mostly downhill or fairly level. WILDERSPOOL CAUSEWAY.

. _ One thing that we cyclists, nature students, archeologists, field clubbists or what we may be, ought to unanimously protest against is the dastardly manner in which the road people have been tearing up the fine old Roman setts between the Swing Bridge and the Brewery Gates. It is nothing short of sacrilege; such vandalism is a disgrace. We had begun to hope, especially when we saw the blue plaque erected in the Brewery wall, setting forth the history of these glorious relics of the past, that this stretch of road was to be saved from destruction. Alas ! as soon as I saw the hot-potato engine, now used as a tar- boiler, dumped in our midst, I knew what it meant. Gone the old Roman Causeway, gone the caves and barrows, the resting places of old British chiefs, and the grand old concertina road will give place to the usual monotonous level. P.S.—Disappointed still and still deceived ! The hot potato engine has disappeared after only a hundredth part of the roadway has been repaired, and the archeologists may breathe again. Lamp time to-night 9.16. Next Saturday 9 25. These times are 20 minutes later than at London.
WESLEYAN CYCLING CLUB. May 18th to Davenham, 22 miles. 21 present. Those who have been unable to get out into the country this week have missed the sight of a lifetime.

r Never in my life do I remember styili a display of hawthorn blessom as we are having this month, and I don't think it will be repeated for another :?0 years. Probably we owe it to the wonderful summer of last year, which ripened the wood of all our perrennial plants. So our run to Davenham by Barnton and Hartford was lined with white hedges all the way. Mrs. Booth made us an excellent alfresco tea, during which a committee meeting was held to arrange the Midsummer concert at Peover on June IZith. The early evening was spent in a ramble down by the river Dane. The splendid Chinese Wistaiia on the 'Ruse front next the Church is not in such grand condition as last year, but such a load of blossom as we saw last May is em,ugh to exhaust any tree. The return journey was made via Lostock and Mere Corner, through lanes even more beautiful than we had seen in the afternoon.

div.head: INDUSTRIAL DEMOCRACY. CHARACTER AND SOCIAL EVOLUTION.
div.p: INDUSTRIAL DEMOCRACY. CHARACTER AND SOCIAL EVOLUTION.

Under the heading "Syndicalism and human nature" I pointed out that although attainable and worth striving for, the ideal ,of industrial democracy could not be materialised by the simple expedient of acquiring possession of the machinery of production. As industrial democracy will be a higher form of industry than that at present prevailing, it follows that it will require for its working a higher individual character in the workers. The whole can be no better than its parts and human organisa- tions follow the same law as all other living organisms. _ _

The possession and democratic manage- ment of industry by the workers will be an indication, rather than a cause of progress. When the workers or a considerable part of them, possess the intelligence and solidarity to produce a more efficient organisation than the present, ownership of machinery will be a matter of course. That is to say, the workers will not first acquire the means of production and afterwards develop the necessary mental qualities in order to run it democratically, but they will acquire knowledge and ownership con- currently. How could it be otherwise? Capitalism exists to-day because it is the most efficient wealth producing system. If all machinery were destroyed it would not take long to build up the system again, pro- vided the characters of the individuals remained about the same. The system can be changed only by the change of character in the _persons engaged in it.

Capitalism as a system tends to prolong its existence by creating an environment which develops characters suitable for its main- tenance. Capitalism means despotism in industry. Order is maintained by placing authority in the hands of one man. The collec- tive movements of every group of workers are controlled by one individual who originates the plan of action and enforces compliance with it. Division of labour is thus made efficient because all the inen work to a common purpose. If the boss were removed there would be chaos because the workers have not yet learnt to work democratically. Industrial despotism implies. the exist- ence of men, arrogant enough to "boss," and of other men servile enough to be " bossed." Men are educated to this and know nothing better and hence feel no shame either in commanding or in obey- ing. Their characters are largely formed by- the circumstances under which they must live. Thus capitalism prolongs its existence. Automatically it produces in its units the qualities necessary for its maintenance— arrogance and servility. Industrial despotism carries with it capitalistic ownership of machinery and appropriation of the proceeds. Men who are not capable of industrial self- organization must submit to the conditions imposed by their organizers, the capitalists. But capitalism cannot go on for ever. The human mind is ever expanding and despotism must give way to democracy. Workers cannot be drilled beyond a certain limit of efficiency and that point seems to have been reached. Modern capitalism educates men as wealth 'producers, but it also educates them to revolt against the monotony and dreariness of their existence. Capitalism will pass, as did the systems of serfdom and slavery, when a more efficient system shall have been developed. The coming system must be industrial democracy or the self-governing workshop. The " boss " will go and in his place will be the chairman or organiser appointed by each group. The small groups of organisations will, of course,be banded together into bigger groups and these again into still greater. The larger. federations will determine the more important principles which affect all the workers and the smaller will settle the smaller matters. Each worker will have two capacities. First as a director in determining by voice and vote the plan of action, and secondly as a worker carrying out his detail in accordance with that plan. In all cases action will be democratic, the individual receiving his instructions from the group, he himself being a director in that group. No man will be at the mercy of a despot over whom he has no control what- ever. Collective ownership of the machinery must come concurrently with the establish- ment of the self-governing group. Men who can organise themselves will be able to see to the equitable distribution of the products of industry. Industrial democracy will spread itself by educating workers in its principles. Men become worthy of self-government as they have opportunities of practising it. And so we may expect that the atmosphere of industrial democracy will tend to develop the qualities of initia- tive, self-reliance, and abnegation to the common plan of action. Democracy will make democrats and democrats will spread democracy. Man's faith in his fellows will increase and human nature will blossom as a flower in the sunshine. Men co-operating industrially will produce more wealth per head than men driven by a despot, and so democracy must thrive at the expense of despotism. When all the brains of all the workers are used in the management, when waste is reduced to a minimum and when there are no industrial disputes, a very efficient organisation will be the result. The world is looking for a new light. Men have grown weary of being preached to and written at—words cost so little I Some day a few enthusiasts will join forces to establish a self-governing industrial organization. , They will study, and try to profit by, the efforts of those who have already made attempts. They will preach democracy and practise it every day, showing to the workers the path they must tread to gain emancipation. They will be true reformers because they will begin by reforming them- selves, and what little they have to say will be listened to with respect as being the words of practical men. My next article will deal with communist and co-operative experiments which have sought the goal of industrial democracy, and some causes of non-success will be con- sidered.
W. BAGULEY.

div.head: THREE WARRINGTON YOUTHS FINED.
div.p: THREE WARRINGTON YOUTHS FINED.

At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, before Conncillor Henry Roberts (in the chair), Mr W Richardson, Colonel Edelsten, Councillor C Jackson Holmes and Mr J Rymer Yonge. Christopher Jarvis, '23, Forster-street, Robert Lee, 43, Forster-street and John Astill, 19, Hale-street, were charged at the instance of the It.S.P C.A. with having cruelly ill-treated a cat. Mr Steel defended and Inspector Dee conducted the case for the Society. Three boys John Bibby, Edward McCoy, and William Sutcliffe aged 12 years and Amelia Morgan, aged 15, of 24, Melville-street, gave evidence to the effect that the defendants chased the cat underneath a cart, where it remained until it was driven out by stones. One of the missiles, a large stone struck the cat on the head, drawing forth blood. The animal dashed out against a gateway, where it was captured by Jarvis, who carried it by the tail to a dolly tub in Astill's yard, where it was drowned. The girl added that when she looked through a hole in Astill's gate she saw the youths dolly the cat. Inspector Dee of the R.S.P.C.A. spole to interview- ing the defendants, who said they had no explanation to offer, except that the cat belonged to Mr Bradshaw, who had removed from Forster-street to Ireland-street, and he had told them to catch the c' t and drown it if it became a nuisance. The cat had b.fn buried in some sand.—By Mr Steel : He unearthed the cat, and found it affected by disease. Mr Bradshaw had told the neighbours to destroy the cat if it got a nuisance, but in no circumstances were they to use cruelty. For the defence Mr. Steel raid the cat, which was suffering from the mange, got to be a ruisance in the neighbourhood, and the youths tried t 3 catch it. It darted under a cart, and stones were thrown at it, not to hit it, but to drive it out. Jarvis carried it in his arms, and it was drowned in a dolly tub. No unneces- sary cruelty was used, and it was really a merciful act to drown the diseased animal. The story of the boys was greatly exaggerated. Several witnesses to support this statement were called. _ .
The Chairman said that by a majority the Bench decided that the case had been proved. The defend- ants would be fined in the mitigated costs of 10s. each.

Borough Police Court. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Smethurst, Bolton and James Evans, and Messrs S Wright, G Pilling, NV Roberts, T Locker and NV Furness. COAL THEFTS. —Two women, Lily Hughes, 166. Back Liverpool-road, and Elizabeth Hartland, 28, Plumpton- street, and two children, Jane Corbett (14). 191, Liver- pool-roads and William Wright (13), 23, Plumpton- street, were charged on the 16th May with stealing 2cwts. of coal, value 2s, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company at Arpley Sidings. The Chief Constable stated that at 7.30 on Thursday evening P.C. Saunders was on duty , in Liverpool-road when he saw the female prisoners in charge of a handcart in which there was coal. He followed them, but they got away and left the coal truck on some waste land. The matter was reported to the police, and it was ascertained from Hilda Smith,that sbortly before that time on Thursday the two female prrsoners and the children were seen near the Arpley sidings, and the boy was seea to get on a truck and send coal down on the sidings, and it appeared the defendants had taken it away.—At the first the prisoners denied the charge, but subsequently admitted it.—The two younger prisoners were discharged, and a fine of 5s and costs was imposed On each of the elder prisoners. A CARTER'S OFFENCE.—Thomas Connerton,l2, Platt- street, was charged with stealing on the 15th inst:, an iron beam value 4s. the property of Messrs. Rylands Bros., Dalton Bank. The Chief Constable said the prisoner was employed by a contractor who carted for Melsrs. Rylands Bros. On Wednesday he was in charge of a horse nnd cart, conveying wire from Dalton Bank to Bewsey and Dallam Forg( s. About 11 o'clock in the morning he went to the house of a Mna Stevenson at 46, Lythgoes-lane, and left the iron bar with her, and she appeared to have taken it to a marine store dealer and sold it. The police did not suggest Mrs Stevenson's husband knew anything about the matter. When the prisoner was arrested the previous afternoon he said he left the works between 11 and 11.30 a.m., and when he got into Lythgoes-lane found the iron bar in the cart. He did not notice it when loading up, end was consequently a bit nervous and he took it to Mrs Stevenson and left it in her kitchen.— I Mr Wadsworth, works manager at Messrs Rylands

Bros., identified the bar as the property of the firm, and said the prisoner had no right to take it from the works.—Eliza Ann Stevenson said the prisoner called at her house last Wednesday, and he had placed the bar in her scullery before she knew what he was doing.— Detective Metcalfe gave evidence as to the arrast of the prisoner, who, in reply to the charge, said,'" I can hardly say that I stole it."—John Allen, who saw the lorry on the morning in question, said the bar of iron was not on the lurry.—Prisoner said the iron was on the lurry, and he did not notice it until be had left the works.—.A fine of 10a, including costs was imposed.

div.head: SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION.
div.p: SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION.
Mr. A. Mounfield on the History of Hill Chile.

The members of the Warrington Sunday School Union organized a pleasant and successful gathering on Saturday afternoon. They assembled in the graveyard at Hill Cliffe to enjoy an open-air lecture by Mr A Mountield,and after the lecture took tea in the Indepen- dent Methodist Schoolroom and held an evening meet- ing. The Rev W Reid prepided at the open-air gathering, and after the hymn " Blest be the tie that binds," Mr A Mounfield gave an address on the history of Hill Cliffe. Taking the Domesday Survey made by William the Conquerer as a convenient starting point, the land was shown to have belonged to a Saxon named Dot,from whom it was given by William to Osbern Fitz Tezzon. This was the earliest documentary reference to Hill Cliffe, but long previous the Romans had been there and one of their great roads bad passed over its crest. To a people who bad used pack horses it hardly mattered that a road should rise over a hill and the Romans followed the habit of making their thoroughfares perfectly straigt. The course of the road (in places marked by stone obelisks), was traced and it was explained that the modern road known as the Causeway was made on the visit of Henry VII., and by entering the town at anew point had changed its centre. Dealing with Norman times, it was shown that Hill Cliffe had passed to Hugh Fitz Tezzon and then to Osbert Flu Tezzon, who took the name of Boyden and whose descendents inhabited ths mast-surrounded Reddish Hall, the site of which could still be explored. Deeds of this period mentioned " Lombroc and "Cressbrook" as boundary lines, an interesting evidence of the long-retained names of the local streams. Geoffrey de Dalton was described as a local crusader whose coat of arm', a Saracan's Head, lingered in the public house sign and another crusader a Boydell was carved in stone in Grappenhall church. Coming t.) the history of Hill Clare graveyard, Mr. Mounfield said it was necessary to set aside a tissue of romance that had been woven around it. Extreme antiquity had been claimed for it, and gravestones engraved with dates of the 14th and 15th and even the 12th centuries were shown or said to exist. But these could only be the most clumsy of forgeries. Those who had foolishly cut them could not have known that gravestones were not in use at such early periods, nor were Arabic numerals in common use. The date of the graveyard was fixed by the deed which recorded the taking over of the land for the purpose of a burial ground, and which was dated 1064. As giving most reliable evidence of the date of the graveyard the lecturer quoted the diary of Matthew Henry, the famous commentator, who tells that he buried Hannah Ambrey in the graveyard in 1709, and adds that her father was the first to be buried there. His grave was not pre- served, but one stone dated from the first year of the graveyard could be seen with the inscription : Maria lieslop. Exit 1064. Other genuine inscriptions dated from 1672 and 1679.
Mr Mounfield referred to the first minister, Thomas Howe, buried in 1695, and described John McGowan famous as the author of" The Dialogue of Devils."

_ The civil war period was described and the operations at Hill Cliffe and. Stockton Heath were sketched. There was no chapel at Hill Cliffe until 1688, but a tradition stated that Cromwell had worshipped there with the congregation (who probably then met in a farm build- ing) on one of his visits. It was pointed out that Cromwell's visit fell in August., 1618. He was in War- ' rington on Sunday, the 20th, lodging in Church-street. , It certainly would be pleasant to picture Oliver taking a much needed hour of quiet amid the glades of Hill Cliffe on a Sunday moniing and then turning in to worship. But the circumstance had to be remembered as the Americans would put it, Oliver wasn't out for his health." He was in the midEt of a nerve-racking ordeal and every moment was of value. The strong probability was that he listened that morning to Thomas Yates in the old Parish Church. Bell Fields was the next point t) receive attention and its eccentric builder Admiral Hoare was described. In retiring from the sea this old sea dog had secured land from Mr. Lyon in an admirably chosen spot and proceeded to build a house alter the model of a ship. The circular lawn, still to be seen, was his deck and from his flag staff in the centre he gave signals to the countryside. He kept his dog, took his observations day by day, rang the bells and observed the dog watch.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May, 25, 1912. BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May, 25, 1912. BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

His servants must approach him with all the ceremony of naval life and sleep in hammocks to take their rest. Admiral Hoare had suggested to Smollett the character of Hawser, Trunnion in his well- known novel. The most famous visitor to Bell Fields was undoubtedly Victoria Alfieri, the Italian poet. He spent two years in England whilst sowing wild oats very freely. He was then in his 21st year and returned to Italy to learn her language and become one of her greatest poets. The nation did him honour by laying his body to rest along with that of Mictucl Angelo under the dome of St. Peters. After the address the company spent an hour in ft ramble and a visit, to Bell Fields. Tea was served in the Independent Methodist schoolroom, and the Rev W Reid presided at the evening meeting. Miss Crosbie of Liverpool gsve an address on " How to interest mothers in Sunday school work "and Mr A Mounileld spoke on " The personal factor in teaching."

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION
(N.A. CENTRE).

The reports from all quarters of last week end were worse than the week previous, although many more anglers WE l'r; out. The Gowy, Dee' Acton Bridge and Long Barn all showed a great falling off. Up to the present we should judge it about the worst close season we have hail for a few yea a ; certainly the set boards are more open this season than they have been in years previous. They now stand with pike 41,1b5.' trout Gozs., eel Sozs., flounder, nil—a very poor record considering the number of anglers who have been out almost every week during close season. However, after the heavy downpour, let us hope for better catches during this week end. Many anglers are taking advantage of the holiday by staying until Monday evening, so with the conditions of angling in their favour and the ordinary amount of luck their should be more than one member asking for the scales. A few more members were made during the week and if the old ones turn up when open season arrives to take out their cards as they did last year, there will be a great increase in the membership. Members who anticipate going north should apply to the secretary for bills for excursion prices. There was fine pike tAW en at Brock during last week and members who were asking for particulars can now have them. We are pleased to say the draw for our late secretary is going off alright up to the present and these who require more books may get them from the club-house or the secretary.

THE GOWY. A fair number of members visited here last week-end but the condition of the stream was all against them. The bott)m was still breaking up and the water being clear and very low sport was almost at a standstill. You could hear of a few eels being taken here and there but that was about all, with the exception of a couple of jtck. The one taken by J Chadwick, jun., weighed almost 31bs. Several members were out for pike and the report from five of them was never a run ; the only consolation was the glorious day for the outing.

div.head: ACTON BRIDGE.
div.p: ACTON BRIDGE.

Several members j)urneyed here both by bike and train, but the sport was at its worst. Members stayed over-night without a stir but intend to give it another trial DOW we have had some rain. This is a water (unless there is fresh now and again) that soon clears and you may see the bottom for at least half- way across. As regards the roach seen dead on top, it it is about the time of the year when they are seen in most canals, and members who were fishing here were of the opinion that they came from the upper reaches and upon makiog further inquiries about this length we learned from Messrs W Brookes and Goodier that they saw roach near Taylor's Bridge and were throwing in feed for them. The roach taken with bread from here was taken by J Bryers, jun. We have had a statement from the North Stafford- shire Railway that the water is again free from pollution. If matters only improve there will be no difficulty in a further increase of members as all local anglers know what a paradise this =al is when in condition.

div.head: CHESTER AND LONG EARN.
div.p: CHESTER AND LONG EARN.

Both these places were visited and here again sport was not to be had. We are still waiting for a flounder from Chester. Several members are spending the holi- day here so we may have to record one before the next notes appear. A.S.
A decrease of 203 in the number of scholars on the rolls is shown in the annual report of the Blackburn Elementary Education Sub-Committee. 'Emigration was accountable for the loss of 118 children.

A man, whose wife and child had died in the work- house, and who had never paid anything towards their maintenance or inquired about them, was sent by the Manchester magistrates, to prison for a month.

div.head: REV. A. M. MITCHELL AND THE LATE MASTER'S SUPERANNUATION.
div.p: REV. A. M. MITCHELL AND THE LATE MASTER'S SUPERANNUATION.
What is a Political Question.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr E L Bent presiding There were also present Mrs Collingwood, Mrs Simpson. Miss Broadbent, Revs T R Matthews and A M Mitchell, Messrs A J Jolley (deputy chairman), W Gill, G Mather, W Houghton, W Furness, R Lee, J A Hughes, G A Allen, J A Rush- worth, W C Brooks, A Bottomley (clerk), 0 Moss (acting clerk). MR AND MRS AWBERY'S SUPERANNUATION. LIVELY SCENE. . . .

The minutes of the last meeting having been read, the Rev A M Mitchell callod attention to the minute extending the period of service to be reckoned in computing the superannuation allowance of Mr. and Mrs J F Awbery, the late master and matron. The CHAIRMAN : Are you opposing the minutes ? The Rev. A M MITCHELL: 1 am asking for one minute not to be signed.
„ The CHAIRMAN : It is a question of for or against the minutes.
The CLERK : The question now is to approve the minutes as a correct record of the proceedings. The Rev A A 1.4 MITCHELL : But I take exception to one of them.

Mr MATHER : I rise to a point of order. It is only asking ; is this a correct record of what took place at the last meeting ? If it is, we are bound to pass it. The CHAIRMAN : Is it your pleasure that I sign the minutes ? (Cries of " Aye "). The Rev A M MITCHELL : I want to move that a certain minute be not passed. I think that is quite in order. Is that so, Mr. Clerk, or is it not? Do you mean to say that no matter what a Guardian has to say in connection with these minutes, they are to be passed like that?

The CLERK : I mean to say this : What the Guardians have to do is to pass these minutes as a correct record of the proceedings of the last meeting. If any member of the Board wishes take exception to any minute, his duty is to give notice of motion that at a certain meeting he will propose that that particular resolution be rescinded.
The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: I took the opportunity of sending a notice of motion which you unfortunately overlooked. The CHAIRMAN: It is out of order.

_ The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : In the absence of that notice of motion on the agenda, I think lam quite right in opening the discussion. The CLERK: The matter Mr Mitchell is referring to has nothing whatever to do with the matter before you. The CH AIRM AN : Nor with these minutes. The CLERK : Nor yet any matter connected with these minutes.

The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL ; My resolution was— Mr. Rusinvottvi : The proper course has been explained to you. The Rev, A. RI. MITCHELL: The resolution was the one extending Mr and Mrs Awbery's superannuation. Mr. IfouGHTON: I move, as a point of order, that we proceed with the next business on the agenda. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: I consider it is very unreasonable— _ _
_ The CHAIRMAN: It is very unreasonable of you to insist like this, when you know it is perfectly out of order.
Miss BROADBENT : I tbought we always had power to revise the minutes. _

Mr. MATHER It is not what we think. It is whet is the law. The law says we are to pass these minutes if they are a correct record. No one disputes the correctness of these minutes. Therefore we should pass them. If any member of this Board wishes to raise a question let him give notice of it and it will be discussed.
The Rev. A. M. M[rcHELL : That is not the order we have followed hitherto.

The CLERK : That, air, is not correct. It has always been your order and no member of the Board can point to any occasion when it has not been thoroughly and rigidly carried out. Mr. HOUGHTON protested that Mr. Mitchell's attitude was a wanton waste of time. For a member of the Board to be so dense that he could not comprehend the routine of the Board—

The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : I intend to give notice of motion—(loud cries of " Chair.") Mr. Manna : Ladies and gentlemen, shall we uphold the authority of the chair or not? I think we ought to stick to the chair. The CHAIRMAN: Next business.
Miss BROADBENT : Is it not allowable to give notice of motion ?
The CHAIRMAN: You can give notice of motion at the end of the business.

At the close of the meeting the Rev A M MITCHELL gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the Board's minute of May Bth, relating to the increased superannuation allowance to Mr and Mrs Awbery, be rescinded.
THANKS. The thanks of the Board were tendered to Crosileld's band for their kindness In entertaining the inmates last week.
OFFICIAL CHANG ES.

The Finance Committee considered the question of filling the vacancy in the Clerk's office, caused by Mr R W Peacock's appointment as relieving officer. It was unanimously recommended tbat Mr R Issell Partridge be appointed first assistant clerk at a commencing salary of £lOO per annum and that M.- W II Bell, deputy-superintendent registrar, be appointed second assistant clerk at a salary of ISO per annum. The minutes were approved. Mr Partridge entered the service of the Board as second assistant clerk in September, WO, and has rendered very efficient service in that capacity. Previously he had been assistant clerk with the under- mentioned authorities :—Plymouth Incorporation of Guardians, Shropshire County Council, Cosfend Union and Rural District Council, and Parish of Bermondsey (London).

div.head: WHAT IS! . POLITICAL QUESTION?
div.p: WHAT IS! . POLITICAL QUESTION?

A letter was read from the Swansea Guardians asking the Board to support a resolution earnestly urging the Government to take up the Criminal Law Amendment Bill 1912, inasmuch as very little time would be required to 'rsal with the matter to pass it into law this session and thus diminish the number of victims and their offspring who become a charge upon the poor rate as the result of immoral traffic in young women and girls. The CLERK remarked that it was not customary for the Board to deal with any questions which they regarded as political. Mr Mazumt proposed that the letter lie on the table. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: Surely a matter of this kind is above politics. I don't think we ought to put it on one side so lightly as that. The CHAIRMAN: We have never before interferred in this direction in political matters. Mrs. CouxsolA'ooD : I don't think it is political. Such a question should be taken up by any Govern- ment—Conservative or Liberal. It is a most important question—one of humanity—and we ought to take it up with great earnestness and support it very heartily. I move that we do so. The Rev. A. M. Mrrcultr.r. seconded. Mr. JOLLEY, as a matter of principle, seconded Mr. Matber's proposition that the letter lie on the table. He sympathised very deeply with the point of view of Mrs. Collingwood and Mr. Mitchell. but they could nct get away from the fact that the question was more or less of a political nature. In matters of party politics they had, as a Board, very wisely abstained from taking part. The Bill touched life on many sides, and, speak- ing quite seriously, they bad to recognise the fact that they could not exclude the elements of party political feeling entering into its consideration. The Govern- ment had not thought fit to accept the measure and be did not think a small authority like that Board, or any other local authority, should meddle in matters of that kind. It was rather a question for public discussion across the floor of the House of Commons. It would be lamentable if the Board committed themselves to Conservative, Liberal, Socialist, Home Rule or any other political views at their meetings. Miss BROADBENT said every decent-minded man must be in favour of suppressing the white slave traffic, and she believed that the Bill had been vGry favourably received by the House. She wrote Mr Hafold Smith, M.P., about it, and in reply he said he was in favour of legislation on the question, but the Bill as it stood was not a very wise Bill and required amending. The mere name of the Bill, added Miss Broadbent, did not mean that it was the best measure. The House as a whole, however, was favourable to its main principles. Alr FURNESS said Mr Harold Smith evidently had a knowledge of the conduct of the Sill. It would be very unwise for the Board to take sides or sanction the Bill as it stood.

1 —.The CgAIRMAN said he scarcely agreed with the vice-. I chairman (Mr Jolley.) If there was anything to he brought forward to get the white slave traffic I suppreseed, it was their duty, as public people, to sup- p.'rt it. He did not wish to influence one side or the other on the question, but somening ought to be done in that direction. The Bev A M MITCHELL said the Board was over- looking the fact that the question was one of urgency. It was a great mistake to introduce the word "politics" in connection with the matter and he thought the Clerk went off at a tangent in doing so. He (the speaker) held these questions were entirely superior to party politics. The CLERK said that had a resolution dealing with the matter independently been brought before the Board, he would have recommended them to refer it to the Association of Poor Law Unions. As it was, the letter wes headed " Criminal Law Amendment Bill," showing that it was supporting a particular measure before Parliament. Be knew all the Guardians felt strongly that something ought to be done, but the provisions of the measure might be entirely antagonistic to their opinions. Mrs. COLLING WOOD If we let the letter lie on the table, it shows that we are not in sympathy with it.

The Bill, although not perfect, goes a long way towards dealing with the question. It is only by going a little way at a time that we can hope to do good. Miss BROADBENT : The expression "lie on the table "sounds contemptuous. By nine votes to five it was decided that the letter hould lie on the table. TIIE INSURANCE ACT. Mr 'MATHER called attention to the fact that the Insurance Act would shortly come into operation. Practically all the Union officials, with few exceptions, would come under the measure and it would make a great difference. The Board had alwrus been in the habit of 'allowing any servant full remuneration during illness, but the Act would knock that off altogether. The question was referred to the Finance Committee.
labas' Church. Annual Sale of Work.

The workers of St. llirnabas' Church have this week been engaged in their annual effort to augment paro- chial funds by means of a sale of work. This year the Curacy Fund and the Church Extension Funds are the special objects to be supported and when the two days' sale was opened in the Conservative Club Assembly Room on Wednesday afternoon the well-laden stalls were evidence of the hard work which had been done in preparation for the event. The stallholders were:—
_ Work stall No. I.—Mesdames Shaw, Birch& Parkinson, Head and Lewis. Work stall No. 2. —Mesdames Handles, Tilling, Hill, Stringer, Oxley, senior. Work stall No 3.—Mesdames Westwell, Sutton and
Bible Class stall.—Mesdames J II G Hollingworth and Oxley, Misses Power, Houghton, Sutton and C Kimberley and Mr B Dimelow (secretary), Men's stall.—Mesdames W Eoyle, T Evans and the Church Officers.

Toy stall.—Mrs Coupe, Misses Bolton, Fry, K Cole and A Fry. Flower stall.—Mrs Hands and Miss A Whitehouse. Refreshment stall.—Mesdames Connell, Jones, Proud, Grounds, Greenhalgh, W Jones and Astley, Misses Normm, S Whitehouse, E Whitehouse, E Jones and Whitehouse.

Dips.—Misses E Hands and II Hassan. The sale was opened by Mrs Henry Roberts. The VICAR (the Rev .1 II G Hollingworth), in open- ing the proceedings, said he was very grateful to all the workers for the way in which they hid worked in preparing for that sale. They bad evidently taken the motto Be and see " to heart, They were those who were prepared to "be " rather than to " see," but generally in the world to-day it was quite the opposite. People were often found to be more eager to "see" than to "be." At the last sale they were all at fever heat because they were expecting a new organ to be dedicated in the church, and when people had something extraordinary to exert themselves for they generally worked harder than under ordinary circumstances. He did not think, however, that there had been any falling off from the enthusiasm which obtained a year ago. The work had been going on slowly and quietly and the organ had been very much appreciated and was a great help to the services. He was very delighted with their organist, who had acted in that capacity for more years than he knew. In regard to the needs of the parish, they were many. The curacy fund had to be maintained. Since last year he had been able to get an earnest and painstaking curate who had made his mark and proved himself to be a faithful and loyal colleague, 'carrying on the good work which was done by Mr Glendinning who left two years ago. The curate had to be paid, and they required £l2O per year for the fund, hence that sale of work. Then there was the Church Extension Fund. The church was not complwed ; they had only as yet got the shell. The transepts and chancel had still to be built. If there was any balance remaining from the proceeds of the sale, it would go to the school fund. The Vicar then welcomed Mr and Mrs. Roberts very cordially. Mr. Roberts he said was a man who felt with him (the Vicar) in the work they were carrying on and many times had helped them in that parish in a quiet way without having been approached at all—and that was one of the most grati- fying ways to receive help. (Applause.) Mrs. ROBERTS paid it gave her great pleasure to be present that afternoon as she sympathised with them in the work they were doing. She was also glad to be there because she was a woman and fond of her needle and she could therefore see and appreciate the result of their labours on the various stalls. She thought they all eejoyed the sewing meet- ings. As women, their time and labour was perhaps the biggest thing they could offer and they gave that willingly with the knowledge that they were helping in a worthy cause. She hoped they would have a successful sale and at the end of the next day—she thought they were brave in having it for two days—she hoped they would have accomplished that which they had set out to do. (Applause). The Rev G A COUPE (curate), in proposing a vote of thanks, said be wanted to assure Mrs Roberts that the people of St Barnabas appreciated her coming there and opening the sale. He included in the proposition the name of Councillor Roberts who bad also come to encourage them. (Applause). Mr W BOYLE in seconding, said he hoped they would have Councillor and Mrs Roberts with them more frequently. (Hear, hear). Councillor ROBERTS in reply said he did not like to be considered an outsider in anything connected with St. Barnabas' parish. The differences between them were not doctrinal differences, tbey were only differ- ences of church polity, They acted alike and felt alike. He was glad to be with them in promoting the common welfare of the people in the ward in which the church was situated. He hoped that with the growing popula- ,tion and prosperity of the district the church would take as prominent and useful part in just the same way as it had done in the past. (Applause). The sale was then proceeded with. THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. The Vicar again presided at the opening ceremony on Thursday, which was performed by Mrs Carleton. In the course of his remarks he stated that the result of the previous day's sale was the sum of £67 14s 10d in which was included a cheque for £25 from Lady Greenall. They were deeply indebted to all who !had helped them. They would require between £3,000 and £4,000 to finish the church in complete style. There was no one in the neighbourhood of Bank Quay more respected than Mrs Carleton and he felt honoured because that was the first sale of work in Warrington which she had opened. (Applause). Mrs. CARLETON, in declaring the sale open, said she wanted to help them in any way she could, because in doing so she derived an enormous amount of pleasure. In the town parishes, where so many people went away to the country it made the work still harder, and they had greater difficulty in meeting the necessary expenses to help on the good work in the parishes. Their two parishes were close to each other, and they both realised the difficulties each one encountered. She gave her assistance quitewillingly and with pleasure. (Applause). The Rev H R WILD, in proposing a vote of thanks, said that Mrs Carleton took a great inteaest in the church life generally of Warrington. The Rev U A COUPE seconded, and the ploposition was heartily carried. The total result of the sale was £l2O 7e ld, the pro- ceeds of Thursday being £52 12s 3d, which included a donation of .£5 from Colonel J Reid Walker. CANADIAN CENSUS. RURAL AND CITY POPULATION.

A special report on the census of Canada taken June lot, 1311, 6hows that the rural population of the Dominion in 1911 was 3,921,083 and the urban popula- tion 3,280,411. In 1901 the rural population was 3,369,018 and the urban population 2,002,297. The increase of the rural population in ten years is there- fore 550,035 and of the urban 1,278,117, which is 16.48 per cent. for the former and 63.3 for the latter. According to this return the rural population of Canada is 55 per cent, of the total population. Indus- trial expansion has been a marked feature of the past decade in Canada and accounts for the extraordinary growth of the taboo population.
ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS.>
UNDER THE BARBER'S POLE.

div.head: FURTHER DISSERTATION ON THE
div.p: A FURTHER DISSERTATION ON THE
BARBER'S SHOP.

Shakespeare wroto in his " Measure for Measure" Act v. scene i. The strong statutes Stand like forfeits in a barber's shop, As much in mock as mark and in so doing enshrined the remembrance of another vanished custom that flourished in the Elizabethan barber's shop. The barber's shop was then a social institu- tion, the forerunner of the club as a place for the exchange of news, where shaving gave the elaborate dawdler an excuse for wasting time. What would such a place be without its standing jests.?

div.head: BARBER'S SHOP FORFEITS.
div.p: BARBER'S SHOP FORFEITS.

The jests took took the form of traps for the unwary,and elaborate systems of forfeits were prepared. Talking of cutting throats, for instance, was so easy a jest for shallow folks that its repetition, became a nuisance and it was put under forfeit. Meddling with things displayed upon the shop board was also put under ban, and so was the handling of razors. Codes of shop laws were hung up and the stranger must study them if ho would steer clear of embarassment.

Which we call surgeons to this day. 'Twere ordered that a hughe long pole, With bason decked should grace the hole, To guide the wounded who unlopt Could walk, on stumps tho other hopt ; But when they ended all their wars, And men grew out of love with scars, Their trade decayed ; to keep swimming They joyn'd the other trade of trimming, And on their p)los to publish either, Thus twisted both their trades together.

This theory that the blended colours of the pole symbolise the blending of the two trades is ingenious and it may be correct. To the same period belongs John Gay's description of a barber's shop, and he too refers to the basins that hung in token of blood-letting. Hie pole, with pewter basins hung, Black, totten-teeth in (rder strung, Rang'd cups that in the window stood, Lined with red rags, to look like blood, Did well his threefold trade explain, Who shav'd, drew teeth, and breath'd a win. BARBERS AND THE STATUTE BOOK.

Quito a long chapter might ba written on the subject o! special legislation touching beards and barbers and stretching from the days when Alexander forbade beards as giving too good a handle for the enemy, to modern prosecutions for Sunday shaving. The Sunday shaving question, it may be said,is very old,the Guild of Barber-Surgeons having put a penalty of 10 shillings upon it in 1592, but they made exception of the two Sundays" next or before Assizes."
Some of the records of the Barber- Surgeons' Guilds make very good reading. There is, for instance the entry at Newcastle- on-Tyne of date 1742. "That no brother shall
shave John Robinson till he pays what he owes to Robert Shafts." Presumably John Robinson went about with a full beard after that.

One of the oldest regulations aimed at the barbers was made in 1422. It declares that they shall not be allowed henceforward to ply their trade in the churchyards. This raises on first reading the comical picture of men getting trimmed for church upon its very door step and the barber doing a big Sunday morning business. The impres- sion may not be incorrect, but the law is probably part of a general prohibition of the carrying on of trade in the churchyards, for in the fifteenth century its was common to hold fairs and markets on consecrated ground. Then there are the laws which placed taxes upon beards and we might travel on to discuss the lore of wigs and periwigs. Butl these cannot be crowded into a sentence, and ' they may give us excuse, if our readers are not tired of the subject, for coining back again by and by to the scented area of the barber's , shop.

div.head: AN OLD DRAWING OF A BARBER'S SHOP.
div.p: AN OLD DRAWING OF A BARBER'S SHOP.
The furthermost figures illustrate the oreration of blood-letting. The patient grasr s the barber's pole while a vein is opened in his arm. The picture is 300 years old.

One of these codes, set in rhyme, belongs to Stratford-on-Avon and may have been familiar to Shakespeare, for though its date is a century after his time it embodies rules that were regarded by the fraternity as being almost as ancient as the trade itself. These are the verses : First come, first 6erved—then come not Tate,

And when an wed keep your sate; For be who from these rules shall swerve, Shall pay his forfeit—so observe. Who enters bere with boots and spurs Must keep his nook, for if he stils ; And give with arni'd heel a kick, A pint he pays for every p ice.

Who rudely takes another's turn By forfeit glass—may manners learn ; Who reverentleFs shall swear or curse, Must beg seven ha'pence from his purse. Who checks the barber in ha tale, Shall pay for that a gill of yale ; Mel will or cannot miss his hat, Whilst trimming pays a pint for that. And he who can but will not pay, Shall hence be sent half-trimmed away; For will he—nil! he —if in fault, He forfeit must in meal or malt. But mark, the man who is in drink Must the caniukin, oh, never, never clink.
The lines are interesting as old English, " First come first served" has passed into proverbial language and " Willy Nilly " appears in its original form in verse five.

THE BARBER'S POLE. Any dissertation upon the barber's shop would be incomplete which failed to attempt an explanation of the time-honoured and mysterious barber's pole. To what age belongs this relic and what the mystery of its .red entwining band?

Along with the pawnbroker's brass balls it is a memorial of the days when almost every trade had its symbol and dangled it forth before the world. The proverb "Good wino needs no bush" dates from the days when a bush was the sign of the wine shop, and the city streets of olden days must have looked a veritable open-air museum in the variety of their symbols. It has been suggested that as the old word for head was poll and polling (or powing) was haircutting, the pole was taken for the barber's sign ; but this hardly commends itself as a solution.

The true explanation seems to lie in the fact that during the process of blood-letting around piece of wood was placed in the hand of the patient. A vein was usually opened in the arm, and during the operation the patient sat with hand outstretched grasping a pole which rested on the ground. In our illustration the barber surgeon is seen opening a vein, and the man sits hold- ing a staff to steady him during the opera- tion. This picture dates backs three centuries, and offers the most likely explana- tion of the pole. A fillet of cloth was twined around it to absorb the blood, and we can still see the fillet entwined round the pole as we have it to-day, though it might puzzle the modern barber to explain why it is there. The cloth band was probably of red as the best colour to conceal blood stains. We assume this from the fact that when the surgeons promoted an Incorporation Bill, after they had broken away from the vulgar barbers, a speech was made in the House of Lords by Lord Thurlow, in which he said that by a statute still in force the barbers and surgeons were each to use a pole. The barbers were to have theirs in blue and white, striped, with no other appendage; but the surgeon's pole, .which was the same in other respects, was likewise to have a galley pot and a red rag, to denote the particular nature of their vocation. We are not familiar with ancient Statute books, but if these things are written there they are interesting bits of law-making. The words "with no other appendage" are illuminated by a statement made by an old writer that the barber-surgeons always hung a bason out at the end of their pole to make it known at a distance "that the weary and wounded traveller might there have recourse A similar statement is made in 1708 in the British'Apollo. The question is asked Why doth a barber at port-hole Put forth a party-coloured pole? And the answer is given. In ancient Rome, when men loved fighting: And wounds and scars took much delight in, Man-menders theia had noble pay,

div.head: DEAN SWIFT'S DISTICH.
div.p: DEAN SWIFT'S DISTICH.

A story of Dean Swift will do to close with. When a vicar in the county of Meath he was shaved daily by the village barber. One day the barber announced that he had taken a litt!e public-house at the corner of the churchyard and that he proposed to carry on the two businesses together. He con- cluded by shying very timidly that he wished in connection therewith to ask a favour.

" Indeed " said Swift "and what can I do to promote the happy union?" And please you' said the barber, "some of our customers have heard much about your reverence's poetry ; so that, if you would but condescend to give me a smart little touch in that way to clap under my sign, it might be the making of me and mine for ever."
"But what do you intend for your sign?" "The 'Jolly Barber,' if it please you, with a razor in one hand and a full pot in the other."
" Well" said Swift " the inscription will be easy," and taking a pen he wrote
Rove not from pole to pole, hut step in here, Where nought excels the sharing —but the becr, This was duly painted and it hung for many years.

div.head: A.M.
div.p: A.M.
DOCTORS' TRADE UNIONISM. "DOWN TOOLS AT ALL COSTS."

At the annual conference of the Railway Clerks' Association, held in London, on SAturday, Mr. Ramsey Macdonald, M.P., said that the black-coated men wanted more combination than other men. They had suffered in the past from being too respectable. Doctors were setting them a good example. They were threatening to lay down their tools, paralyse society, and leave them all in the cutter. He was not saying whether they were right or whether they were wrong, but he was simply citing the hard facts of the case. When doctors had adopted trade union methods, what man among them ass so respects.ble that he could reject trade union methods? The aid of black-coated workers was needed to help the Labour party in the uouse.of Commons.

CHINA'S STREET NEEDLEWOMEN.

China is, perhaps, the only country in the world where one may have his garments mended on the street while he waits. In nearly all the principal cities of the Flowery Kingdom native sewing women are to be seen seated on low stools, perhaps on the sidewalk, mending articles of masculine wearing apparel. The accomplishments of these street seam- stresqes are somewhat limited, their efforts with the needle being confined, as a rule, to "running." Other branches of needlework are practically unknown to them. As a consequence their efforts are better appre- ciated by natives than by foreign travellers. They are never short of patrons among the Chinese tradesmen, for these are:often natives of other districts and, having come to the city to engage in business, have no one to mend a rent for them. Their wives being left at home, they are glad to employ the street needlewoman. For this class of customers the skill of the sewing woman answers every purpose. _ _
_ As a rule, they are wives of boatmen and labourers who live in the house-boats which line the creeks, and their needles are a great help in the task of earning a living. ANCIENT INKSTANDS.

An inkstand that was probably in use three thousand four hundred-odd years ago is now exhibited in a Berlin Museum. It is of Egyptian make, and is supposed to belong to the eighteenth or nineteenth dynasty, or somewhere about 1500 8.C., though its real age can be judged only approximately. It is made of wood, and has two compartments, an upper one provided with two holes, one for black and one for red ink, and a lower one for holding reed pens. The black and red ink are certainties ; for some still remains, in a dry condition, within the receptacles. Another ancient inkstand is supposed to have been intended for the use of a school- boy. It would certainly hold ink enough for a schoolboy's needs; for it has no fewer than four ink holes. Both inkstands were found at Thebes.
THIS WEEK'S STORY. PAT'S SPOTLESS CHARACTER.

Pat Delaney applied before the magis- trates for a licence. On being asked if he had anyone in court to speak on behalf of his character, Pat looked round and said : "Yes, your worships,' the Chief Constable, " Why, don't know the man." Pat said: "Your worships, I have lived in this town 20 years, and the Chief Constable doesn't know me. Isn't that good enough for yez ? If I'd had a bad character he would have known me." Pat got the licence.

div.head: NEW COUNCIL SCHOOL,
div.p: THE NEW COUNCIL SCHOOL,
WHY THIS DELAY P

At a meeting of the Warrington Education Com- mittee on Monday evening, Mr. J. Upson called attention to the following minute of the School Management Committee:—" It baying been reported that the desks for the Evelyn-street Council School were ready for delivery, but that they could not be accepted owing to the building not yet beirg com- pleted, authority was given for the payment to the makers of storage rent for them at the rate of 425. per week, together with the cost of cirtage, and it was resolved that the attention of the Sites and Buildings Committee be called to this effect of the delay in com- pleting the building." Ile said the committee were entitled to know w hy they were called upon to pay for the storage of furniture which they contracted to receive b rig since. First they were told that the schools would be opened in the new year, then that they would be opened at Easter, and now they were to be opened in July. The School Management Com- mittee, btlieving that the schools would be opened somewhere about the time first mentioned, bought the furniture rnd now they had to pay for it to be s:ored. They ought to know who was responsible for the delay. Was it the contractor, the architect, the Surveyor, or the committee ? Aldermln BOLTON ; Why do sou buy furniture before it is wanted?

Mr RINGDON thought a charge of two guar,•as per week for storage was very heavy. Councillor JENKINS said that as there were over 600 desks they took up a considerable amount of room, and two guineas per week was therefore a moderate charge. Canon STEVENSON said the committee bad always been led to suppose the school would be ready for opening on hunary Ist, and it seemed to be their duty to have the furniture ready. TI ore were no doubt good o 'uses for the delay ; it did not rest with the committee. The minutes %ere carried.

div.head: An Adult School Celebration.
div.p: An Adult School Celebration.

The Adult School movement is assuming enormous proportions in various parts of the muntry, and seeing that its objects are the making of men with a broader outlook on life, that all denominations are welcome, that it is unsectarian and non-political and that it recognises divine nature in all humanity, and that the social side of man's existence is one of its cardinal features, no wonder that it has gained a firm hold in Warrington. As will to seen by advertisement, the parent school in Academy-street, is being visited on Sunday next by Mr. William C. Braithsvaite, 8.A., LL.B., of Banbury (the chairman of the National Council of Adult Schools), and a cordial invitation is extended to any of our readers to the morning school, mixed adults, or the fellowship meeting in the evening when Mr. Braithwaite's address will be "Reality in religion."

div.head: BRAVE YOUTHS HONOURED.
div.p: BRAVE YOUTHS HONOURED.

At Runcorn, on Monday, the chairman of the Bench banded illuminated certificates of the Liverpool Ship. wreck and Humane Society to Albert Wright Aston and Frank Burkhill for gallantly rescuing a boy from the Big Pool on February Ist. Ihe resewe was more creditable from the fact that Aston bad to crawl along the ice to get at the drowning boy and was in the cold water for ten minutes. Alderman Norman,the chairman of the Bench, heartily congratulated the youths for the bravery they had exhibited.i He was glad to think that Runcorn was never lacking n people of their stamina, who were ready to lend F.% helping band to thole in danger. Aston, who also received a postal order for 20s, returned his thanks, and said he hoped that others who took risk would be as fully raw arded as he had been. Burkhill also expressed his thanks.

A resolution was passed at the quarterly meeting of Leigh Labour Party, when 2s trade unions were repre- sented, against the introduct,on of the military during the miners' btrike as an basult to the workers.
