div.head: SCHOOL CHILDREN'S TEETH.
div.p: SCHOOL CHILDREN'S TEETH.
A Striking Feature of the Medical Officer's Report.

The salient features of the report of the Medical Officer of Health (Dr J Coote Hibbert) on school hygiene, were commented upon at the meeting of the Educa ion Committee on Monday evening by Air If I Kingdom in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Medicalinspection Committee. He pointed out that one of the most important features arising out of previous reports was the necessity of alterations from hygieni,2 and sanitary point of view in some of the schools. Recommendations were forwarded to the Sites and Buildings Committee and he was glad to acknowledge the help they gave in many cases in seeing that improvements were carried out. There were, however, notable opportunities for improvement still left, and he hoped that if there was any member of the com- mittee who had not read the report, he would do so most carefully. (I Tear, hear). As regarded the work of the committee, their powers had finished when, acting upon the advice of the Medical Officer, they , drew the attention of the Education Committee to the defects as they existed. They could then do nothing further ; the responsibility rested with the full com- mittee. The work of the school clinic was progressing satisfactorily but there was no doubt that it ought to have been done years ago (Hear, hear). He was only voicing the views of his committee who's he said that they were glad to he associated av'th work of so remedial a nature. They had decided to further extend the clinic so as to deal with dental defects, and that that was necessary would ho seen when he drew attention to the report, which stated that 82.2 per cent of the children had imperfect teeth, in other words that four children out of every five of school age had teeth that that (light to have been attended to before this. Defective teeth were often the cause of illness and suffering—they caused abscesses and a poisonirg of the system—and the only qualms he had was as to whether the the Waif and means at the disposal of the committee were adequate to cope with a growing necessity. Mrs. JACKSON HOLMES seconded.

Mr PLINSTON drew attention to a minute which read as follows : " Resolved that the Sites and Buildings Committee be recommended to make arrangements whereby the School Medical Officer may be consulted when the plans for new schools or alterations to school buildings are under consideration." It seemed to him to be a strange thing that the Medical Officer had no voice in the matter at the time of the erection of the schools. They found in the report that more than one school of recent date was adversely criticised by the Medical Officer. Mr R T FAIRCLOUGH said the Medical Officer laid much stress on the disadvantages of the pail closet system and appeared to cast a slight on the school managers. The fault, however, rested with his own , deparlment, as the closets were not kept as clean as they ought to be. Alderman BENNETT said it appeared to him to be foolish to consult the Medical Officer after the schools had been built. It was like locking the stable door after the hcrse bad been stolen. (Flear, hear). lie regarded the repott of the School Medical Officer as one of extreme interest. The evils they had to remedy were cinsiderable, and he was rather afraid that they were only playing with the fringe of the question. At the same time it was something to know that they had made a start, and he had no doubt that with such am enthusiastic chairman as Mr Kingdon, bicked up by the Medical Officer—a gentleman they were proud to call their official—(heme, hear)—and with such a committee !steady progress would be made, and that a great deal would be done, so that the rising generation would have a chance of growing up not only intelligent but healthy. (Hear, hear.) Mr KING DON agreed that it was right that the plans of a new school should be submitted to the Medical Officer in order that the committee might have the advantage of his experience. The minutes were then agreed to.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
ANTI-VACCINATION.

The extraordinary case at L 3 rum Petty Sessions, rerorted and commented upon in last week's issue, reminded me of personal experiences of what I sup- pose may be fairly regarded as the genesis of the anti-vaccination movement —I mean the imprisonment of the protestirg Keighley poor-law guardians, (or, as they preferred to call themselves, guardians of the poor). I have not at band the mears of votification, but I suppose that must be not far short of 10 years ago. I 'lewd the "martyrs of the cause "—plain unlettered men— tall the story of their persistent refusal to enforce the Vaccination Act, and of their incarceration for contempt in disregarding a mandamus of the High Gault; in fact, I reported it for a Yorkshire paper. When, a few years ago, relief was afforded by law in the form cf %hid' the defend- ant in lest week's case at Lytrm bad availed bet self, I was on a paper in the sister county, and so great was the immediate rush of applicants for exemption certificates that extra courts bad to be constituted and sittings arranged srecially to deal with the eager crowds. EMIGRANTS' CHAPLAINS.

At the meeting of ministerial if embers ef the Liver- pool Wesleyan Distiict Synod, the Rev. Jcseph Jackson complained, in referexce to the difficulties in transferring emigrants, that a great deal af presely- tieing was taking place on the ships by agents of the 8 P.C.K. Well, being myself a Nenconformisr, I certainly do not hold a brief for those against whom the charge was lerePed ; but I have acme little knowledge of the subject, and can testify that not all] the clergy who act as chaplains on ece.igranYships are sheep-stealers. So far as I have olserved, they are drawn from the ranks of working clergy who need rest and change and are willing to serve in this way for the expenses of the trip. Of the two mln m I have known to take advantage of it, one who has repeatedly done so tells me that he makes it a real holiday. He is candid enough to confess that he performs the duties in a somewhat perfuoctoty manner—that is, he simply conducts the EOIVICCS rrquircd of him, and no more. Once, said be with a chuckle, he went to Canada in that way, ad obtained from the railway people a pass which ecab'ed him to travel over the country and vi,it many places of it. terest, 'and," he added significantly, "if I were on the staff of a newsparer, that's nothing to what I would do." This rev, gentlemen, holder f several high degrees, "knows the ropes," and has enjoyed many good holidays at nominal cost to himself ; hut, from what I know of him, lam quite satisfied be has done no proselytising while 60 employed. To be sure this does not aisprore Mr. Jackson's statement; it merely- shows that, if by "agents of the B.P.C.K. " we are to understand the chaplains appointed to emigrant ships, all these clerics are not " limit that way." ANGLING.

I fancy I have previously stated that I always read with peculiar interest of the doings of the Warrington Workingmen's Angling Association. They are of a goodly company and in a glerious successien. It is true that B)ren referred to Isaak Walton as a cruel old coxcomb, acd to the art as a solitary vice, but the poet himself did a little fishing; so we need nct take his supposed strictures seriously. Among devotees of rod and line, moreover, may be mentioned Dean Swift, Walter Scott, Tom Hughes,Chatles Kingsley, Matthew Atnold, Davy, Chantley, Dryden, Gay, Paley, Nelson, Hook (of course), Mark Pattiscn, LivingstonP, John Bright, and an innumerable multitude of mere or less noted personages. I know thete are others -who see nothing at all in angling, and even laugh to scorn the art and all wedeed thereto. A while ego, I was in 'Wharfedale, and passing along by train caught sight of an enthusiastic angler diligently fishing under heavy rain ; and the cemments made by some of my fellow passengers were—well, to say the least, they were uncomplimentary to the craft. DIFFICULT TO PLEASE. - - - -

The incidental allusion to Wharfedale inevitably suggests Mr. Carter netts, the irrespiessible angling expert of that district, who in a charactistic sketch wrote ROlllO time ago : " Some men dime are who flout the gentle craft Lecause they are dissatisfied with its material results.Hodgkinshaw was one of this type. Hodgkinshaw somehow never was satisfied with any- thing. Once we persuaded him to go fishing with us, because he said he wanted some fun, and we said he would be sure to get plenty cf fun out of it. Well, before we'd been down by the liver ta 0 hours an infuriated bull had pitched him head over heels clean over a five-feet fence, and be had tumbled into a deep bile in the liver, and been dragged cut with a landing-net sl aft with a great deal cf difficulty ; and a farmer's dog had chased him over a couple of fields into a bog; and he bad had a stand-up fight with a gamekeeper; and had been stung by a wasp; and had sat down en an ant's nest, while the ants happered to he at bocce, with plenty of !cisme time en their banes to give Lim a warm welcome. Well, no reasonably minded man could have expected more fun than that in such a limited space of lime, and yet, when we chanced to ask him bow be was enjoying himself, be just yawned wearily and growled :----" Lcok here, boys, I haven't seen a blessed fish caught yet. This game's a blamed sight too slow for me; I'm goirg Immo." And he went. He was not satisfied with the fun he had had and the esplanade]] that the conditiors were against catching fish. div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

W hams Customs.—The children have an utcleoiable stake in Whitsur t'de, more particularly perhaps in the North and Midlands, where the charming sight of marching Sunday school scholars nay be witnessed year alter ye tr. 'the weather may mean much to young n and maidens ; t, the child ea it means everything. It can make or mar their festival, a time-honourtd observance which carries the mind Lack to the early 3 ears a the last century, when customs were vastly different from what they are to-day. Gone is the <lop erel verse which used to be sung, and vanished are other Latures which were often more objectionable. It seems strange now to mild cf sums paid for " spiced cakes and se." fer refreshments for the teachers, and there are also items shown in old records for " pennets and wine." With the spread of education there has been a corresponding improvement in the atnicsphf re of Sunday rchools, and in some places the Whitsuntide processions partake of the character of a general or township institution, towards which all classes and creeds extend a benevolent and kindly interest. Free Holidays for Working Girls.—The growing appetite for holida3s is common to all classes. This was recognised by the Queen, when her Majesty desired that the wester porti, n of the fund raised by the Merles as a Coronation gift, should be used fur pro- viding a holiday home tor working girls. There are few in regular employment in the tovros who, do not contrive nowadays to get some or other little clung° during the summer, but a goodly number of London working girls ;vat 133 able to obtain an ideal fortnight's holiday at Barn House, Whitstable, which has been taken by the Queln for this purpose. div.head: NEW KING AND QUEEN OF DENmARK.
div.p: THE NEW KING AND QUEEN OF DENmARK.
new ruler of Denmark, King Christian X., was born in September, 1870, and is the eldest son of the late King. He married in 1898 Princess Alexandrine of Mecklen- burg. There are two children, Prince

Christian Frederick, born in 1899, And Prince Knud in 1900. It will be reinembaled that the new King represented his father at the Coronation of King George. His younger brother is the King of Norway, and the husband of Princess Maud.

div.head: PREVALENCE OF SUICIDE.
div.p: PREVALENCE OF SUICIDE.

The reference to General Booth recalls the report (surmarised in last Saturday's " Examiner ") on the fifth year's working of the Anti-Suicide Bureau by the Salvation Army. If ary consolation whatever be desirable from such statistics, perhaps it may be dis- covered in fact that matters are in this respect better at home than they are abroad. I read scmewhere a while ago that, greatly as the rate of suicide had increased in this country, it lags far behind that of France, and yet finther behind that of Germany, where the pace of advancing prosperity is swiftest. .!!. striking case is that of Japan, which has been investi- gated by the Russian statistician Tarnowsky. During the past fifteen years, which have seen the final stages of the turning of Japan from a simple and natural int, a complex and industrial community, suicide has increased over fifty per cent In four years the number of American suicides has actually doubled, the number in 1910 being 12,608 As will have been gathered from the foregoing, the explanation is that we have drifted into an existence more comp'ex and more divorced flora the instinctive ways of mankind than Ram world has ever known ; even to live with an independent income is more of a strain than to struggle for a hying a century ago. I for one heartily echo the hope for a return to saner ideas and ways of living.

div.head: TELEPHONE SERVICE.
div.p: THE TELEPHONE SERVICE.

"The Times" of Tuesday ssys :—Mr. Herbert Samuel gave yesterday a very Inteiesting and, npon, the sviuole, satisfactory account of the huge and Taried business now carried on by the Post Office. Mr Samuel does not affect to deny that the telephone service has been far from satisfaztory, but be pleads great difficulties con- nected with the transfer of the business from the National Telephore company, arrears of capital expendi- ture, and complications due to climatic conditions. these excuses must be snowed considerable weight. still it is evident that the vigorous grumbling of the public some time ago was neither tnjustiflable nor wanting in utility. me more stringent instructions issued to ept raters and the closer supervision now pro- vided are the fruit of public complaints about slackness in using apparatus actuslly in existence.

a time, the first: come a being selected from the four senior clubs belonging to the London Girls' Club Union. They will be able to stay a fortnight, as guests, entirely free of cost, rave for the railway fare—s few shillings —which they must pay for themselves. New and Old Materials for Summer Wear.—Every week, manufacturers rend out novelties in tie way of materials for sum .ner wear, and these with old frierr's in new guise make a bewildering variety from which it is difficult to make a selection. All cotton goods have, this season, a silky appearance, due to the mercerising process which is now applied to every cotton material. Especially noticeable for their good appearance and modest price are the cotton poplins., that make, with pipings of oontrasting colours, the daintiest of summer coats and skirts. The browns in these goods are in beantiful shades, and look well with string coloured macrame lace or crochet. Cotton Shantung,s tussores, and foulards, are all mercerised, and each can tbe recom- mended for economical, yet dainty summer wear. Women Pastors.—ln some of the Pretestant cantons of Switzerland, the poorer parishes and villages are seeking women pastors, as it seems the remuneration is so poor that clergyman cannot be found to accept the ollice. It was in these circumstances that the Rev. (Miss) Gertrude von Petzold, an M.A. of Edinburgh Univesity, offered her services, and it was her applica- tion which first suggested to the Byood of the Canton Orisons, the throwing open of the vacant churches to women " clergymen. It is understood that this lady has since accepted a similar position at the Unitarian Church, Small Heath, Birmingham, and there seems to be a difficulty in finding suitable women candidates in Switzerland to undertake the work of the Church. There are plenty of applicants, but they mostly lack a University education and theological training. That is a difficulty which will no doubt soon disappear, and in this, as in other professions, it sill be the case of women doing the same work as men for starvation pay. Colour Combinations.—Certainly distinction in dross may be attn'ned this year with very little expense by those who can cleverly combine materials and colours. The latter more especially give excellent results when carefully cossidered. Blouses of a different colour from the coats end skirts with which they are worn,lend themselves to novel and pretty effects. Take for instance, a nut brown taffetas salt, which may have a mauve ninon blouse, embroidered in shades of brown, and be worn over a purple silk slip, or a citron green blouse of thin silk, shot with eggshell blue,which looks exceedingly well, ellen worn with a raven blue suit. Many colours are worn with black this sewn, more especially bright shades of violet, eterry colour, and green. Pipings of green satin look well on straight plain black dresses.

A Delightful Sommer Fabric.—The new Trop'cal "Vyella ' is very sure of a hearty welcome, for it means a 6UffielenCY of warmth without weight, and therefore a greatly minimised danger of chills. The latest batch of patterns forms a charming callection, calcuLted to please the most exacting and fastidious. For undergarments, sleeping suite, dressing gowns, blouses, shirts, costumes for every kind of sport, after- noon dresses and for the nursery, the new Tropical " Vyella " indeed comes as a bacn and a blessing for summer wear. Buttons and Blouses.—Buttons fairy an important. rut in the scheme of many tailor made. In some instances they form the only trimming, And much ingenuity is shown in their arrangement. They have now invaded the domain of the lingerie blouse, and are used in quite a novel way to form patterns in conjun- Lion with eyelethole embroidary. Tne buttons used are quite flat, stout a quarter of an inch in diameter, and are most effective in black linen on while lawn. Ths blouses are further trimmed with pipings of black linen doe n the fronts and on the cuffs. Thie idea is capable of great variety, and might hs carried out to advantage in colours on white grounds.

div.head: WIDNES CHEMICAL EXPLOSION. THE INQUEST.
div.p: WIDNES CHEMICAL EXPLOSION. THE INQUEST.

A month ago a gloom was cast over Widnes by a terrible explosion at Muspratt's Chemical Works result- ing in the death of five workmen. The theory advanced then as to the cause was that during the process of elevating a huge dryer or vat into position by means of jacks, the friction caused by the movement ignited some carbonaceous matter at the bottom of the dryer, causing a violent explosion. Huge tongues of flame shot out from underneath, and six men sustained extensive burns. One of the men, named Groome, of Princes-street, was burnt to death on the spot. The remainder were taken to the accident hospital. Abrams

div.head: "TITANIC" INQUIRY.
div.p: THE "TITANIC" INQUIRY.

Society was strongly represented at tho " Titanic " inquiry this week, when Si Cosmo Duff-Gordon completed his evidence, and Lady Duff-Gcrdon gave hers. In her evidence she said she had quite made up her mind to be drowned when she and her

husband were pitched into boat No. 1. She denied the stories of her escape which appeared over her name in a newspaper, and said the signature was a forgery. Our photograph shows Lady Duff-Gordon (on the right) and Sir Cosmo Gordon (in the doorway) leaving the inquiry.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn B3ard of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday. Mr Joseph Spruce presided over a good attendance. After the minutes of the previous meeting bad been confirmed, the Chairman said they would all no doubt be aware that since the last meeting an old and valued officer of the Board had passed away in the person of Mr Thomas Riley, formerly relieving °fiber for the Frodsham District. He thought that it was only proper that they should pass a vote of condolence with the family of the deceased. Mr. Linsker sen., in moving the motion said he did so with deep feeling. Mr Riley was, as many of them were aware, a most valuable officer to the Guardians for a good many years, and a more conscientious man in the discharge of his duties he never came across, lie was a man who had his whole heart in his work and was very considerate to those who came under his charge. He used a large amount of discretion in sift- ing deserving cases from the undeserving ones. He was ever ready with his sympathy where it was needed. He was not only a very a-,tive officer for the Guardians but he took a deep interest in the parochial life of Frodsham and had been church warden of his Parish Church for many years. The deceased gentleman was I also a good advi=er to those who needed advice and he (the speaker) felt sure all the people of Frodsham would regret his death. Whatever his opinion was on any matters he at ways fearlessly expressed that opinion in the most courteous terms. (Hear, hear). Mr Davies, in seconding, said he endorsed all that the previous speaker had said. He had known Mr Riley all his life and quite agreed with all that bad been said. INir Woodward supported end said he had been associated with the deceased for about 20 years and had always found him a most reliable and conscientious officer who never failed in the discharge of his duties. He had never known him to put

and Davies died the same night, Moss expired next morning, and Marsh died a few days later. Coroner Brighouse adjourned the inquest until yester- day in order that the survivor, Michael Haley, could attend and give his version of the affair. Mr T W Stuart, general technical manager (United Alkali Company) and Mr J Morrison, district manager, were present. Mr J W Knowles represented the Inited Alkali Company, and Mr B B Peters appeared for the relatives of Davies and Moss. _

Mr. Jackson, senbr JIM. Inspector, watched the proceedings Haley was the first to give evidecce so as to allow him to get back to hcspital. He said he lived at 2, Margaret-street, and had been employed at Muspratt's for 13 years. He knew the drying bed in the chlorate house, and this had been raised in a standing position by two jacks to turn it over. The order was given to lower and this was done. He recollected nothing after huge flames shot out.

_ Thomas Dolan, labourer, 40, Victoria-street, said that three minutes before the accident he was sent by the foreman to get two iron plates as wedges. While away he heard an explosion and hurried back. The place was in flames, and several men were burnt. John Donaldson, foreman in the chlorate room, said he bad washed the floor in the drying room in the morn- ing, end while engaged in filling kegs with chlorate at thuee o'clock, close by, he saw tongues of flame shoot out of the dryer. In answer to the Coroner, witness "suggestd that the accident happened in conseqoence of some irregularity in the flooring. Thomas Minton, works engineer, said the dryer had been in use 23 years. Ile had given instructions to Abrams to raise the dryer, with the intention of chang- ing the leaden bed. AD.. liedley, the works manager, made an inspection, and when he saw the presence of rivets on the bottom orders were given to lower it and let it rerca'n. Shortly after he heard a shout of fire and hurried to the fire station on the promises. In answer to the impactor, witness raid he bad never noticed any unevenness in the floor, but in his opinion the cause of the accident arcse from acme potash lying in the bricks on the floor. Mr. Hedley said he quite agreed with Mr Minton's evidence. Ile believed the fire was caused by friction through lowering the dryer. The Coroner : Had you any idea whether the irregu- larities in the floor might lead to trouhle ? Mr Iledley : I was not aware of any, or I would never have allowed a man to go near. Mr Jackson said that the explanation was a reason- able one. Expert opinion keld that chlorate would not explode by itself. Experiments had been carried out, and it had been found that coming in contact with wood dropping on it was sufficient to cause it to explode. This had happened at Muspratt's. The firm had taken great precautions, and their rules were in advance of the regulations required of them. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death " in each case. The Coroner intimated that the firm bad paid full wages up to the present, all funeral expenses, and £1,176 had been paid into Court for compensation.

div.head: I\IINIIIUNI WAGE -AND SHIRKERS.
div.p: I\IINIIIUNI WAGE -AND SHIRKERS.

- - In the annual report of the Blackburn Trades Counci representing 25,000 trade unionists, Mr Philip Snowden declares that there is the prospect of establishment by Jaw at no distant date of a legal minimum wage for every industry. The only serious objection to the enforcement of a legal minimum wage was the alleged difficulty of abuse by shirkers and malingerets. This no doubt was a danger, and no workman believing in the principle would minimize the seriousness of the objec- tion. If employers and employed gave the system an honest trial most of the apparent difficulties would be found to have no real existence. The workman wanting a wage for doing nothing was a curse to his class.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
CRITICISMS AT THE ANNUAL MEETING.
President and the Sporting Spirit.

Considerable interest centred in the annual meeting of the Warrington Football Club, which was held at the Co-operative Hall on Thursday evening. There was a large attendance, Mr. T. Locker (president of the club) presiding. There were also on the plat form : Messrs T. Barker, T. Barnes, jun , T. Bunch, T. Davies, W. Hewitt, E. Osborne, J. H. Wh itham, T. Pemberton (treasurer) and B. Ashton (secretary). Mr. J. F FOSTER, in moving the adoption of the secre tary's report, said it was not as satisfactory as they would have liked—in fact they had passed Oro ugh one of the worst seasons experienced for many years. One pleasing feature of the report was the optimistic note it sounded with regard to the future. The secretary stated that they had several young men coming forward, and they had done well in their trials. They hoped those young men would mature and turn out good player 3, because the club required them. (Hear, hear.) They wanted not only a couple of heavy, fast forwards, but a couple of brainy half backs, and a new three-quarter line. Their full Lack position was one of the strongest in the Northern Union. In Renwick, Mclntyre and Tilley they had three of the best full backs in the Union. He hoped that by develop- ing young talent they would bring the club back to its former position. Mr T P BRADSHAW seconded. He said that under the circumstances the committee and the club had done remarkably well. He thought the members were entitled to an official report on the Frawley case. (Hear, hear.) They felt that the committtee intended to carry out the bargain they entered into, and that they acted in a sportsmanlike manner in granting Frawley permission to play for the Australian team when be was wanted. On the other hand Frawley should have considered the bargain he made was binding. Mr. E. ENGLAND congratulated the team upon the equipment of the ground which was now superior to the grounds of most clubs in the Northern Union. With that, his compliments to the committee on the year's doings must cease. The report was one of the most meagre ever presented ; it contained practically no informaiton. The saying applied to the E cottish race—that the Lord endowed them with "a good concert of themselves "—seemed to be a fitting description of the members of the committee in seek- ing re-election after the way in which the club had acquitted itself in the playing sense. (Laughter.) He fully expected a few resignations. (Applause.) For several years there had been something lacking in management and organization and the club had not reached that high standard of play which they had a right to expect frcm a club of its standing. The few matches he saw last season impressed him as the worst exhibition of football given by the Warrington team since the Northern Union came into force. The club had been adopting the policy of seeking players all over the world ; it had proved most expensive and in some respects not worth the candle. He suggested they should now go in for the encouragement or local talent. Warrington lads had the true patriotic feeling towards their town and would play with greater zest. They had notable examples of the success of that policy in Widnes, Wakefield Trinity and, in years gone by, Runcorn. Mr GEORGE Slurrn characterised the report ass very weak one and expressed the view that the corn mittee had been behind it. The difficulty of turning - out two teams ought not to be a subject for comment in the report of any Northern Union Club. He com- plained that the members had not been treated as members, particularly with regard to the Frawley case: they had been treated as dummies, and had heard nothing except through newspapers. It was very brave of Mr Osborne to take up the cudgels on behalf of the club. (Hear, bear.) The Secretary ought to approach the Northern Union and ask them to go into the case. The SECRETARY: All that has been done and it has occupied a great amount of time. The report was adopted. Mr. S. WRIGHT moved the adoption of the treasurer's accounts. He said the report was typical of Mr. Pemberton than whom there was no better treasurer in the Northern Union. (Applause). Mr: MADDEN seconded.. - . - .

Mr. H. ROGERS asked for an explanation of the item of £375 for transfer fees and delegates' expenses. Mr. BRADSHA W called attention to a loss of £l2 7s. on the sale of Great Northern Railway stock. He suggested that in future the club should invest in Warrington Corporation stock which paid 3i per cent, and there would be no loss in realizing on such bonds. Mr. W. MASON said that in a club like that there should be no speculative investments. Their money should be invested in gilt-edged securities and he could not conceive that in these days of industrial strife railway stock could be regarded as such. Warrington Corporation bonds were always worth 20s. in the £. He noticed that £162 6s. 10d. had been spent on refresh- ments for players (local and visitors) and committee— about 50 or CO people each week. Turning to the bar account he found that the total amount spent by the 1300 members who attended matches regularly week after week was only £lB9 175. Id. He did not grudge money for legitimate refreshment but in a year when when the financial prospects were not bright, the item might have been reduced. Mr PE3IBERTON explained that £334 14s 2d was paid for transfer fees, and payments to various clubs for junior players, while £42 was spent in expenses of the committee, interviewing players, and expenses of players. With regard to the Great Northern Railway s'ock it was considered when bought as sound an invest- ment as the club could have, and the committee could not be held responsible for the depreciation of railway securities in troublous times. The account for refresh- ments to which Mr Mason had called attention included an extra £7 for entertaining the Australian team, £5O 17s Gd for hotel expenses for teams and committee, and refreshments for players and committee (including visitors and practice matches), cost £9l 15s 64. The accounts were passed. • THE PRESIDENT.

Mr. H. ASHTON moved the re-election of Mr. T. Locker as prtsident. He was whole-hearted in his enthusiasm for the sport and had not only afforded the committee excellent advice from the commercial stand- point but had gained much useful information for them during his travels in the country. The proposition was carried with enthusiasm. THE PRESIDENT AND LOCAL TALENT. WANT OF ENTHUSIASM.

The PRESIDENT, who was heartily applauded on rising, as id : I can assure you that it is a position I have not sought, and I should have been glad had the selection fallen on other shoulders. You are fully aware that the president's chair is no easy one, and the weight of duty and responsibility ever tends to become more burdensome so that while I am fully prepared to do my very best for the club during my term of office I must say defiaitely that the termination of the next season must see the close of my presidency. I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to say a few wards upon a topic whi ch has occupied my thoughts very seriously of late. MI en the club was first formed almost every member was a player and now no players are members. It is a startling fact that out of a membership of 1,300 we have not one single player, and yet a large proportion cf the members must be of an age to play the ga me. How is this ? Surely we can- not regard it as a satisfactory state of affairs. Is the present generation of young msn more cOntent to watch the game than to play it. I ask this question without any attempt to answer it bat this I will say that if members will come to the practices in August next and have a try at the game the corn mittee will give them every possible encouragement. Warringtm, with its large population, local enthusiasm, junior teams and works competitions ought to be extremely rich in local talent. As things are, however, our eyeshave been in " the ends of the earth" for class men, although it is extremely probable that much latent and undeveloped talent is at our very doors, and perhaps among our own members. My strong advice to the young members of the club is to come down to the practice games. Eleven aside matches, which could easily be arranged if suflioient memb era would turn out, besides adding much to the interest, would enable you to discover what skill you possess, and possibly many hidden "stars" would be revealed. If I may venture to express my opinion, I think the primary duty of the committee should be constant watchfulness for signs of talent among the young players of the town, and the pro- viding of ample opportunities for its development. And now I want to say a word about the young players themselves, or rather about the spirit in which some of them approach the game. I think it may be truthfully said that most of the past generation of players played the game for the game's sake, and not for what they could get out of it. Yet last season one junior, who was in the recent works' competition, asked £lO to sign on, although he did not prove good enough for our "A " team. I only mention this to show the mercenary spirit of some of the young players of to-day, and we, rs a oornmittae, rather resent this, for no one can say that the Warrington Club has not in every case treated its players generously when they have been triers and good useful men, and I say this unhesitatingly after 15 years' experience. do not want to be unduly pessimistic, but I really think, and have cause to think, that there is not that perseverance, that desire to practice and train, and to excell among the young men of to-day, that was found BO prominently in an older generation. Is it that they shirk the hard work, which is so indispensable to success? Of course I recognise that we cannot grow a class team largely of local talent in a day, and must proceed on our present lines for the time being. But what I should most like to see the aim of the club would be a desire to promote a local patriotism and enthusiasm around a team composed of Warrington lads. This I believe to be quite possible. The two

things necessary to bring it about are, an enthusiastic, businzss like, watchful committee, and a better sport- ing spirit among the young players and young men generally of the town and district. Mr. LOCKER concluded by expressing satisfaction that Mr. Ashton had agreed to act as secretary for another season, and paid a warm testimony to the worth of both secretary and treasurer—two of the beat officials in the Union. SECRETARY AND TREASURER.

It was intimated that Mr. John Winstanlev, who had Seen nominated for the secretaryship, had withdrawn. Mr. HARVEY moved that Mr. Ashton be re-elected secretary and Mr. Pemberton treasurer. They were well tried officials and the club could not do better than retain their services. Mr. MASON seconded. He said the club bad now a year in which to look about and find a new secretary and he hoped the question would not be sprung upon the members so suddenly at the next annual meeting. , He suggested that three months before the meeting the position should be advertised at a salary, the best rcan who applied to be appointed. The proposition was unanimously passed. Mr. ASHTON, in returning thanks for his election, said the financial position of the club was not such as to warrant the appointment of a paid secretary. It would cost at least £250 a year to get a decent secretary, maintain an office and staff. It would be better to have a secretary who would do the work through love of the game rather than for a sense of duty. He (the speaker) felt that if he had been withdrawn from all official work at this juncture, he would not have been doing his duty to the club which he had always tried to encourage Ile wished to see the club placed on a strong financial footing. Rugby football was one of the finest institutions in the country and if they could only bring about a reconciliation between the Northern Union and the English Rugby Union and make it one sport and one body, it would recieve as much patronage as the Association code. Some reflections had been cast on the Warrington committee but he , could assure the members that they were an exceed- ingly hard working body of men. Mr Ashton then went into the history of the Frawley case and said the committee expected Frawley to carry out the agree- ment he made as a gentleman and a sportsman to sign on for Warrington before February Ist to qualify him- self for the cup-ties.
AUDITORS. Messrs W Webster and 0 GRIN were re-elected auditors.
COMMITTEE.

Voting by ballot for the committee resulted in the election of the following :—T P Bradshaw, 3b3; T Barber ; 310, E Osborne 328 ; T Bunch, 314 ;J F Foster, 230; J H Whitham, 218; T Barnes, jun., 217; T Davies, 212. The unsuccessful candidates received the following votes.—George Smith, 203 ; .1 Lodge, 141 ; W Hi 11,125 ; S Wright, 100; J Bibby, 75. 111.srs W Hewitt and W Nevins did not offer themselves for re-election. BENEFIT FOR DICKINSON.
Mr J. A. BLucE proposed - "That U. Dickinson have a benefit match.

Mr. T. BARNES, jun., seconded. A lengthy discussion ensued as to advisability of having the benefit match next season. It was stated that in view of the financial position of the club,it would be better if the matter were deferred until the next annual meeting. The general feeling of the meeting, how- ever, appeared to be in favour of having the match in the forthcoming season. Mr OSBORNE said he was sure that there was no desire on the pirt of any member of the Committee or mem- ber of the club to shelve the question of granting Dickinson the benefit. They had, however, to consider the financial position of the club. They lard spent over £1,600 on the ground in the last year. They owed about £273 and he felt that if they could clear that away during the next season Dickenson ought to have the match. They wanted, first of all to rid the club of that liability. If they had the money he would say at once that he should have the math next season and he felt sure every com- mitteeman was anxious to give him the match. If the mocey was forthcoming and they could see their way to give it him they would do so. (Hear, hear). After further discussion it was decided that Dickenson should have a benefit and that if finances would allow it, the match was to take place next season. (Applause).

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
SHOPLIFTING AT ST. HELENS.

SIX MONTHS FOR THEFT. Margaret Milburn, a married woman, of 61, Glover- street, was on Saturday dealt with by the St. Helens magistrates on two charges of theft. It was stated that she had stolen sixteen shillings' worth of goods from the Palatine Stores, belonging to Mr. Robert Robinson,and twelve shillings and sixpence worth from the tall of Charles Oxley in the market. Detective Anders found a number of stolen articles in the prisoner's house, and said that she had pledged a number of things. The prisoner pleaded guilty. When arrested she was wearing an underskirt with very large pockets intended for the reception of stolen goods. She was sent to gaol for six months.

SEPTUAGENARIAN'S FATAL INJURY. Mr Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at St. Helens on Monday. on Abraham Davies, seventy, of 51, Brook-street, who died on Friday last from an injury to the hand. Mrs Jane Smethurst, daughter, said her late father was a blacksmith. About eighteen years ago he lost his right eye, and had since been employed as a litter's labourer at Messrs Pilkington Brothers' sheet glass works. Ho worked all right until the commence- ment of the coal strike, when be was stopped. On Saturday, Marchl23rd, he was breaking up boxes in the backyard, and four days afterwards he showed witness his band, the palm being very much swollen. He said he had run a nail into it when he was breaking up the boxes. She applied poultices, &c, but a doctor had to be called in. lie died at the Providence Hospital. Dr. Fox said that the scratch on the hand set up blood- poisoning, which brought on exhaustion and bronchitis, this being the cause of death. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: Evelyn-street Headmastership
div.p: Evelyn-street Headmastership

Sir,—ln the Daily Mail" of May 22nd it was reported that at a recent meeting of the Oldham Education Committee strong objection was raised to the appointment of a teacher, from a place no further removed than Moston on the ground that he was not a native of Oldham. The clerk expres=ed regret that the committee had no power to intei fere with the 1002 Act under which the appointment was made by the managers and instead of by the com- mittee. The inference to be drawn is that under the 1902 Act, all teachers should be appointed by the school managers. Is it not a fact that the Evelyn- street school managers hare not ever been consulted with regard to the recent appointment. ENQUIRER.

Sir,— On the question of the Evelyn-street head- mastership and the resolution proposed by Mr. Upson at the meeting of the Education Committee on Monday, I fail to see the wisdom of trying to correct one wrong by creating another. The teachers are going the wrong way about the matter. If there is any injustice it is not of the Education Committee's creation and they would be better advised if they agitated through then- Teachers' Association for the injustice to be put right on comprehensive and national lines. I copied the following rertinent, if unsavoury allusion to a similar question from the "Life of Dr. Pryde." The reproach that used to be levelled at the nation (Scotland) that it was too clannish and acted too much on the principle of its own unsavoury proverb of 'Keeping its an fish guts for its am sea maws ' eel tainly cannot be brought against the educational aystern. For many years the obvious and earnest endeavour has been to secure the best man DO matter from what part o the globe he may come." Dr. Pr,yde also tells us in hi " Life " thst he once got an application from a teacher in which this sentence occurred : "I am a married man and a Christian also." A woman wrote in ;favour of her husband and said he was specially fitted to fill the post if school janitor because he had a sister who was married to a gentleman whose father had been a teacher.—Yours, etc., SA.TCHEL.

div.head: N.S.L. and Health.
div.p: The N.S.L. and Health.

Sir,—Tbose cf 119 who have bad the pleasure of meeting Mr. Dukes, the writer of the interesting letter on the N.S.L. and Health, know that all he says or writes, is worthy of close attention, for it expresses the thoughts of a man earnestly anxious for social improvement. Without following him into a complex discussion as to the influence of economic conditions upon our modern life, may I agree with him on his aversion to war? We all wish to live our lives in peace. But to-day Demos is king. Financial magnates, kings or em-erors do not make war unless the majority of the citizens of a nation are roused. In the long run wars are largely the responsibility of peoples, nut of rulers, and to-day the sheer con- understanding of some international problems may bring about an explosive demonstration of feeling. .Now under which military system are we most likely to avoid war—a system of a professional army with the nation's citizens separated from knowledge or experience of the possibilityZof war, or a democratic system by which the whole able-bodied population will be liable to be exposed to war, if they unwisely give way to headstrong counsels? The course of the world's policy to-day is in favour of letting the voter know that if he shouts for war, he must bear its risks in his own person. Towards the ideal of peace the N.S.L. is pressing, but only by a road which recog- eises the facts of modern history.—Yours Ac., B. S. TOWNHOE. Ipswich. 2.lrd May, 1912. Sir,—Mr. Dale in his reply to my criticism of the speeches of the N.S L. lecturers, says that my ques- tions were so mixed as to leave him in doubt as to the real position. Allow me k) make my position clear to Mr. Dale. I am opposed to the N.S.L. upon principle. My complaint is that the speakers did not state the basic principles of the N.S.L., but confined their remarks to the effects of military trainiog upon the physique. The point at issue is : Are the N.S.L. out for com-

pulsory military training as a Meal; of -building up a higher physical standard, or are they out to establish a force for home defence with the object of liberating the standing arnly for foreign aggression ? I hope this is clear. If the former, then I claim that there are other methods whereby we can achieve the object with less trouble and without breeding the Jingo spirit. If the latter, then I claim that the workers should seriously consider their position before joining. Let us take a view of the position and suppose the worker to be compelled to undergo military training. Now military training demands a stamina upon which to build. Those who know anything of the conditions of labour know that the high intensification of labour in the modern workshops renders those employed more fitted for a quiet holiday and rest at the seaside than for the physical exertion demanded by military train- ing. This is more like to oppress the worker rather than to build him up. What is more, the N.S 1.. offer to take their recruits into the fresh air for training in return for services rendered. Where is the advantage? If he worked for an equal length of time,as that devoted to military training, with his earnings he could choose his own method of recreation. You say that it is important that the rising generation should have good food and should masticate it properly. I agree. But bow are we going to do it—by military training? Bad food and rotten teeth are the result of what? Lack of

discipline &c.? Not a bit of it. Rather lack of funds. Masticate food properly—half an hour for breakfast and walk to the check office and back again. Take the general labourers who outnumber all others. Why do they eat bad food? Why are they physically degenerate ? Why do their wives have to go to work and neglect their domestic duties? Why do women work and men tramp the streets unemployed? It is because they lack industrial organization, not military training. In other words physical regenera- tion is an economic problem, which goes to the very root of capitalist society. Again, if the expansion of capital demands that we, or rather the capitalists, should conquer fresh markets, which means an extension of our military operations, does it not also mean increased exploitation of the workers to provide protection for the new interest? This is why the N.S.L. advocates compulsory military training. I believe in a citizens' army, not as a means of liberat- ing the standing army for the purposes named but as a means of its abolition. There is a loan of .t 200,000,000 to be raised in London for the purpose of commercial enterprise in the East and those responsible for this venture assert that military protection will be required to safeguard increase of interests. How can it be got.only by an of military forces as advocated by the N.S.L. ? The attempt to cloak these problems under the guise of physical training and offering to young and inexperi- enced men the luring bate of a week or two's holiday should not pass notice. I deplore the condition of the workers of the country, but I am yet •to be convinced that military training is the way out.— , Yours, etc., CHARLES DUKES.

ADJOURNED INQUEST.-FULL REPORT,

div.head: Coroner's Severe Censure.
div.p: Coroner's Severe Censure.

A verdict of ‘. Accidental death " was returned at the adjourned inquiry held at the Warrington Police Station yesterday into the circumstances attending the death of Mr. Joseph Witter Houghton, aged 51, Holes-lane, Woolston, one of the best known farmers in the district who sustained fatal injuries in a collision between a motor car and a governess car in the Chester-road last Saturday week. At the same time the jury found that there was considerable negli- gence on the part of Mr. Victor G. Roberts, the driver of the motor car, but that it did not amount to culpable negligence. Mr. Roberts was severely censured by the Coroner.

I It will be recalled that Mr. Houghton, with his wife and daughter, was driving to Stockton Heath in a governess car at about 8 o'clock on the evening in question. Just as the " battle neck connecting the Wilderspool and Chester roads was reached, a motor car, owned and driven by Mr. Victor G. Roberts, I approached from the opposite direction. There was a conflict of evidence as to the rate at which the mctor car was travelling, several witnesses describing it as "terrific," g while Mr :Roberts himself put it at 20 mileslan hour. After striking the kerbst ,ne on the left hand side of the road the car swerved and crashed into the governess car. Mr Houghton was so severely injured that he was conveyed to the Infirmary. It was found that he was suffering frcm flacture of the skull, concussion of the brain, and shock. He never rallied and the news of his death cleated a painful sensation in the district where he was held in the highest respect.
into the trap ?—I cannot say. It came straight across the road.

Did it catch the trap on the off-side corner ?—lt caught it on the off-side, certainly. The front corner, if I may so term it ?—I have not seen the trap since the accident. It did not come into the full side of it. Do you think it caught the pony ?—I did not see it. The Coroner : I vas very well acquainted with your husband. He often served on juries hnd assisted me in my duties and I want at this moment to convoy to you how sorry lam that you have lost your husband. I want you to accept my honest sympathy. Hilda Haslaca Houghton, daughter of the deceased, said the governess car was about the middle of the narrow part of the road when they saw the motor car approaching. She could not gauge the di6tance between tho two vehicles. The motor ctr seemed to go very near to its cyan side and then dash acrots the road into the govetneei car. The Coroner : Can you form any opinion as to what speed the car was going at ?—No, It was going very quickly.

div.head: INQUEST OPENED.
div.p: INQUEST OPENED.

Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner, opened the inquest at the Police Station on Monday evening. Mr Roberts was not present, but he was represented by Mr Steel. Mr Ridgway appeared for the relatives of the deceased. The Chief Constable (Mr M Nicholls), occupied a seat alongside the Coroner. Mr NVilliam Isaac was foren_an of the jury. The Coroner in his address to the jury, said a report bad been issued by the police in which it was stated that at 7.50 p.m. on the lith inst,.Mr Houghton accompanied by his wife and_dauglater, was driving a pony attached to a governess car along Chester-road in the direction of Walton. Along the same road a motor car, ED 269, driven by Mr Victor Roberts who was accompanied by Mr Frederick Mullins, travelled in the opposite dirn- lion. The motor car, according to witnesses, passed along the centre of tte road at a dangerous pacs. When entering the narrow part of the highway which con- nected it with Wilderspool-toad the car sa enrol to its near aide, caught the kerbstone, and thcn dashed across into the pony and trap. The pony was knocked down and badly injured. All the occupants were thrown out of the governess car. Mr Houghton was rendered unconscious. Dr Law, Dr Joseph and Dr Harold Joseph were summoned to the scene, and found he was suffering from concussion of the brain and shock. He was removed to the Infirmary, and di. dat 3.30 on Saturday afternoon. Several eye-witnesses stated that Roberts was travelling at a very dangerous pace, and appeared to have lost control of his car. In order Oat there might not be any misapprehension as to the cause of death a post-mortem examination Lad been made by the surgeon at the Infirmary. That night he pro- posed to hear evidence of identification enabling him to issue a burial order and the inquiry would ttea be adjourned to a date suitable to the jury. Mr. Richard Denham, solicitor's managing clerk, Hazel Dene, Green-lane, Padgade, said the deceased was his cousin and was 51 years of age. Ile had been very intimate with the deceased and had known him all his life. He last saw him alive and in good health a few days before the accident. He visited him frequently at the Infirmary and be was present when the deceased passed away. The inquest was then adjourned until Friday morning. Mr. Steel said the roadway where the accident happened was very narrow and dangerous and he sug- gested that the Coroner and jury should visit the place and see for themselves. Although plans might be pro- duced they could not sufficiently indicate the place and its surroundings. The Coroner said views were very useful indeed but he liked to make the view after he had get the evidence of witnesses, not before, because the witnesses went into the box and gave their statements and when they had heard the evidence it was most useful to go down to the view and make the witnesses tell the story again on the spot. Arrangements could be made for them to be taken there. _ _

Mr Steel said he agreed because he wanted the view to bees effective as possible. The Foreman : We all agree to that. The Cor.mer : It looks as if it is going to be a lengthy case. Mr. Steel pointed out that the trap and the car were stored for the inspection of the jury. It was decided that these should also be seen.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S INQUIRY. A MYSTERIOUS MOTOR CYCLIST. Was the Car Racing ?
div.p: YESTERDAY'S INQUIRY. A MYSTERIOUS MOTOR CYCLIST. Was the Car Racing ?

The remarkable degree of public interest in the proceedings was evidenced by the crowded attendance at the Borough Police Court when Mr. S. Brighouse, County Ccrouer, opened the adjourned inquiry yester- day inaurning. Accompanying the Coroner on the bench were several local justices of the peace. Mr.,T. Ridgway represented the relatives of the deceased,and Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for Mr. Victor G. Roberts. The Chief Constable (Mr. M. Nicholls) watched the proceedings on behalf of the police.

div.head: CAUSE OF DEATH.
div.p: THE CAUSE OF DEATH.

Dr G S A Bishop, junior house surgeon at the Infirmary, said he had made a post mortem examination of the deceased and found an extensive fractu e of the skull. Death was due to laceration of the brain. The Coroner : The result of the fracture? Witness : No sir, I think the result of a blow on the back of the head. This man died from injuries received ?—Yes, from injuries received to his head. MRS. HOUGHTON'S EVIDENCE. CAR GOING AT "EXPRESS SPEED.'

Mrs Houghton, widow of the deceased, was then called. She stated that at 7.30 on the evening in question her kusband, her daughter, Hilda Haslam' and witness left home in a governess car for the purpose of visiting a sick friend at Stockton Heath. They decided to go along the Chester-road. Mr Houghton was driving and witness was sitting opposite to him, with her daughter in front. The horse had belonged to them about 17 years. It was a very quiet animal. They had passed over the railway crossings when they first saw the car. She could not define the exact place where they saw it, but the governess car had turned into the narrow part of the road. The C,roner : You cannot say how far it was when you first saw it ?—I cannot tell. It came so quickly, it was in such a short time. Was your husband keeping to the near side of the road ?—He was keeping to his own side. As the car approached you, did it seem to be going in the middle of the road, on the off-side or on tha near side ?—lt seemed to catch the footpath on its own side and swerve right across to our side. How near was it to you when it did that ?—I could not tell. . .

Was it a long way off or was it just approaching you? —lt was so that I knew we could not get out of its way —that it was bound to come into us. Did it come into you ?—Yes. You could see there was going to be a smash ?—Yes. What did your husband do ?—He pulled the pony up with both hands and said" Good Lord."

--.- Then the car was into you ?—Yes. Have you a vivid recollection of what the car did— whether it struck the pony, the shafts or the wheels ? No. I only remember being tossed up and then coming down again after having so many bangs. I don't remember any more. I Living at Woolston, you will see any number of cars passing between Warrington and Manchester ?—Yes. Can you give Us any idea as to what rate this car was travelling at ?—No. In miles per hour ycu cannot. Can you form any Opinion as to the rate it was going at by saying "slow," " moderao," " quick," or " very quick " ?—I should say it was going at express speed. Is there anything else you would like to tell the jury in connection with this matter ?—No, I don't think so. Mr. Ridgway : Do you remember whether there was sufficient room between your trap and the remainder of the road ?—I don't remember. You remember that your trap was close up to the left side ?—YeF, I remember we were on our right side of the road.

Questioned by Mr. Steel, witness could not give any definite statement as to the respective positions of the trap and the car when the car was first noticed. In answer to the Coroner Mrs. Houghton said she could not indicate the spot to the jury if she visited the scene of the accident. _ .

Mr. Steel : You say.the car caught the footpath and then swerved across tc) your trap. Do you think if it had not caught the footpath, that it would have gone through without catching you ?—I don't know, at the rate it ,aas travelling. Was it catching the footpath that caused it to come

div.head: "IN A ZIG-ZAG WAY."
div.p: "IN A ZIG-ZAG WAY."

Frances Hammon, wife of William Hammon, 4, River- road, said she was in the na-ros part of Chester-road when the accident occurred. The trap was going very slowly on its right side. She saw the motor car come round the bind of the road in a zig-zag way. Neat she saw the tam, of the motor car on the footpath, after which it crashed into the governess cc!. Asked to descrite the speed of the car, Ns itness said it was going very fast. Mr S esl : Is it not a fct that anybody coming down the Chester-roe.d on his own side would naturally come into the middle of the narrow tart ?—Yes. And it would require a bit of zig-zagging to get cn to his own side ?-1 cannot say. Are you quite clear that both the hack wheels of the car were on the footpath ? From the appearance of it, I should say I am. How long were the wheels on the footpath ?—lt was all over in a second.

Mr Steel : Do you think Mr Roberts or the drier of the car was trying to avoid the trap ? The Coroner : You know very well it is impossible for her to say, because efore she could anscNer that questin sLe ought to be able to put herself into the mind of the driver.
I%lr Steel : Did you Fee the driver doing anything to the car here cvms no time to see. It was all over in a second.
"A TERRIFIC PACE."

Jc,Ln Honey, warchouseman in the employ of Messrs Richmond, thing at 31, Chester-road, said that at 7.50 he had !nit gct out of the " bottle neck " and was crassing ttiver-road on his w .y.home. The first thing that attracted Lis atttntion was a great cloud of dust and then a motor cycle approached. Immediately altorwards he saw the n otor car.
The Curoner : At what rate vaire the motor cycle and the car going ? Were they both going at the same speed ?—No. lhe car was slightly gaining on the cycle as .it approached me.

, At what rate did they seem to te going as they approached you 9—.ltates of speed are very difficult to estimate but, as a moderate man, I should say about 25 miles an boor. Were they going slowly, moderately, gently, quickly or what ?—I should say they wee going at a terrific paco. As they passed me the motor cycle was still in front.
--- -- Did 30u turn round and watch ?—I turned round and walked Lacy.

Why ?—Knowing the place as well as I do, passing it many times a day, 1 was convinced that something would happen. Taking into consideration the pace at which they were going and the geography of the place, you came to the conclusion that something was going to happen and you turned Lack ?—Yea.

_ . Further questioned witness said the motor cycle was nearly in the centre of the road, but slightly towards its own side. The motor car was on the right-hand side,but it would have to take up that position in order to pass the cycle safely. Witness did not see the car pass the cycle—as a matter of fact, he did not think it did pass it. The Coroner : What did the car do as it came to the " bottle neck "7 —lt gradually swerved into the " bottleneck."

After it got into the" bottle neck " what happened ? --I could not tell you. My view was obscured by the formation of the road and dust. Have you seen cars go more quickly than this car along the Chester-road ?—I cannot say more quickly. I have seen them go as quickly. The Chief Constable pointed out that whereas the witness had stated that the car was going at a terrific speed, on the other hand he said it was travelling at only 25 miles an hour, which was not by any means a terrific speed. Could he explain that away? Witness : I should term it a terrific speed. The Coroner : If you knew as much about cars sal do, you would find that when you come to villages and have to bring yourself down to ten miles an hour, there is not one man in 100 who can do it. He could go at 15 or 18 miles an hour and I don't think anyone would judge he was going more than ten. "SHOUTS Or JUBILATION."

Martin Hughes, warehouseman in the employ of the Firth Co., living at 41, Hamilton-street, said he was on the right side of the Chester-road, going in the direc- tion of Walton. The motor cycle and the car were travelling at what he regarded as a very terrific pace. When both the vehicles got to within 15 yards of where he was standing, the car passed the cycle on the right hand aide of the read. Just as the car was in a line with the cycle he heard one of the occupants, Frederick Mullins, begin to shout " Hurrah." As they passed the cycle, the cyclist also shouted " Hurrah." "1 thought ' added witness, "that it was in jubilation at the car out- distancing the bike." The Coroner : Did you come to the conclusion that they were racing each other ?—Yes, sir. The Coroner : They both seem to have gloated over the victory. What did the car do then ?—As it was nearing the narrow part, of the road, it swerved right into the kerb stone on the left hand side, and almost toppled over. Then, almost on the instant, the jolt on the kerbstone and the driver's sudden swerve of the lever to the right, caused the car to take a half turn and it went in a slanting direction and came on the top of the governess car. Can you say whether the driver of the motor car, from the time you first saw him to the time he went on to the governess car, slackened his speed at all ?—No, sir. In my estimation, I say that when he rassed the motor bike he increased his speed. Mr. Steel : When you saw the motor car trying to pass the cycle on the right-hand side you were under the impression that it was doing something wrong ? Yes, sir. You were under the impression that he Should not have gone round that way but that he should have COMA along the kerbstone ?—I think I should have come on my proper side to pass the motor bike. That is still your idea ?—Ye, sir. Could the shout of "Hurrah " be heard by the people roundabout ?—Yes, I believe it could You say the car was going at a terrific pace. Give us some idea of the speed it was travelling at.—l don't think he could have put any more power into the car than he did.
What would be the speed ?—I should put it down at close on 40 miles an hour._

Not more than forty ?—I should not say so. Going down Chester-road you say he was going at 40 miles an hour, and had his full speed OD ?-1. say when he was passing the motor bike. Do I understand that when he passed the motor- cycle and got into the narrow part, he increased his speed ?—Yes. The Coroner: If anything, he went faster. Mr Steel : Was there much dust about ?—No sir, I should not think so, after the recent rains. Can you tell the jury at what speed he would be travelling when the motor struck the governess car ? I have come to the conclusion that he checked his speed through coming into contact with the kerbstone. The foreman of the jury : Did the car go on to the footpath, or just touch the kerb ?—lt did not go on to the footpath. It grounded the kerb. At the time of the accident where was the motor cycle ?—lt was following the car and would have to pass the wreckage.

div.head: "A MYSTERIOUS MO TOR CYCLIST."
div.p: "A MYSTERIOUS MO TOR CYCLIST."

- ----• The Coroner : We cannot find that motor cyclist. I wish we could. Another accident in which a motor cyclist was concerned, took place at such a time and place that one could reasonably assume it was the same cyclist, but we cannot find him. Mr Steel : We wish we could find him. Fred Holland, clerk in the employ of the L. tt N.-W. Railway Company, living at the Conservative Club, said he and a friend named Harry Wright were in the narrow part of the road, on the way to Walton, and saw the governess car in front of them. Witness next saw the motor car turn the bend of the road. At what rate was the car going?—l could not say, sir. Was it going gently, smoothly, quickly, or at a terrific pace ?—lt was goiag far too fast for the part of the road. Did you come to some conclusion as to what was happening ?—Yes, I thought the driver had lost control of the car. Did you come to that conclusion in consequence of the way in which the car was being driven in the road ? —Yes, sir. . .

Did' the car go straight down the road or from one side to the other ?—From one side to the other. And came into the trap ?—Yes. I see you told the police that you thought the car was coming into you ?—Yes.

Did you see a motor cyclist pass you ?—No. Neither before nor after the occurrence ?—No. The Coroner: He is a mysterious person is this motor cyclist. Do you really want him very badly Mr. Steel? Have you tried to find him ? Mr Steel : Yes.

i You have no idea who t was y—No. Charles Reginald Parry, clerk in the employ of Messrs Greening, living at ?A White-street, who was also walk- ing in the direction of Walton, said the car was travelling rapidly and he concluded that the driver had lost control. It swerved to the left, then try the right, back 'to the left, and then collided with the trap. Victor Roberts was driving it. By Mr. Steel : He did not notice the car catch the kerb stone.

The Foreman : Do you know where the car passed the motor cycle ?-1 did not notice a motor cycle. Ilarry Burden, engine cleaner, Lower Walton, said he saw the motor cycle travelling 10 yards in front of the motor car. They were both going at far above the average speed—at from 30 to 40 miles en hour. When he passed witness, the motor cyclist was about 50 yards from the " bottle knock." Witness heard one of the men in the cat shout to the cyclist, but he could not tell what he said. The motor cyclist eventually slackened spe3d but the driver of the car seemed to have lost control and passed the cycle. The car dashed into the kerbstone, cut a letter w and crashed into the trap. A Juror: Where did the motor cyclist go to ?—He stopped for a minute or two and then went straight on through the town. John William Cartveri2ht, cabinet maker, Moore, said he was cycling alcng Walton-road, near the Ship Inn, when Mr. Roberts's motor car passed at about 25 miles an hour. The car had to come to a dead stop at the Stag Bridge as the gates were closed. Witness was first to get through the gates, in accordance with the usual rule, and was passing the last row of houses on the Chester-road when a motor cyclist overtook him at 40 miles an hour. He was followed,!at a distance of 10 yards, by Mr. Roberts's car which was travelling at about the same rate. When the car reached the narrow part of the road it swerved to the left and caught the ken bstone. Then it " flung "straight into the trap. By the foreman : The cyclist appeared to slacken speed.

div.head: "PLENTY OF _ROOM."
div.p: "PLENTY OF _ROOM."

John Morley, farm labourer, Padgate, said the motor car was traveling at a great speed when the smash occurred. There was plenty of room for it to pass the trap. The driver was doing something with the brakes —witness coult not tell what—but he seemed to have lost control of the en altogether. Witness did not see a motor cyclibt. The Coroner intimated that he did not intend to call several witnes who could corroborate wl,at others had already stAted. The Court then adjourned for lunch, and it was stated that the Coroner, jury and a number of witnesses would inspect the scene of the accideut during the interval.

DRIVER "PERFECTLY SOBER." The first witness after the aljournruent was Inspector Stuart. He said he was in Wilderspool-rat when he heard a noLe and saw pelple running towards Chester. road. On going to the scene of the accident he saw the motor car. The deceased had been taken into a house and Roberts was attending to him. Dr Law and Dr Joseph were sent for and ordered his removal to the Infirmary. Witness afterwards spoke to Roberts. The Coroner : Was he drank or scher or in what conditkn ?—He was sober. Quite sober ?—Yes, sir. At what time ?—About ten minutes after the acc;dent.
At any rate, he was perfectly sober ?—Yes, sir. You asked him for his licence and be produced it ? He did.

--- -- Did you ask him ho A' the accident occurred ?—I did What did he say in reply.—lle said "I did not see the trap till I got near to it. I tried to apply the brakes— I don't I.iaow whether I did or not. I lost myself." The Coroner : The Chief Constable informs me— and therefore I can assure you—that there are two other officers who would corroborate the Inspector with reference to the condition of Roberts. If it is not con- tradicted, you will have to take it as a fact that he was sober.
Mr Steel : I have Dr Law as well to speak on that matter.
v[croß ROBERTS'S EVIDENCE. "NO RACING." _

Victor G Roberts, Broomfield, Grappeohall, who described himself as a medical student, was then called, and said he had been driving the car about five years. Prior to that, he had had a motor cycle. On the night in question be was driving from Frodsham, accompanied by Frederick Mullins. When they got to Stag Bridge the gates were closed and they had to pull up. Afterwards they proceeded down Chester-road. Mr Steel : At what speed were you travelling down Chester-road ?—lt would not be over 20 miles an hour. Some mention has been made of a motor cyclist. Did you see him ?—I saw him in front. Was he always in front of you, or did be pass you ? No, he dian't pass me. When you approached the "bottle neck " did you do anything to the car ?—Abont ten yards before reaching the first limp post I put the clutch out. Was the clutch out from that time until you entered the" bottle neck "?—Yes.
. - When you got into the "bottle neck," what side of the roadway were you taking ?—I had to take th 3 centre becr.use there were some people on the left side of the road.

When you got into the " bottle neck" you got from the middle of the road to the side ?—Yes. What did the car do ?—I did not see the trap until I got round it (the corner). Directly I saw it I pulled the car to the left to give it as much room as possible. What did the car do ?—lt caught the kerb and seemed to jolt on it. I immediately applied the hand emergency brake. In order to apply it you had to lean down with your right hand ?—Yes. That would mean you had only one hand on the steering wheel ?—Yes. . . _ . _ _
And the left hand at that ?—Yes. When you caught the kerb stone what happened to the car ?—lt swerved right across the road. In the circumstances did you do all that you possibly could ?—Yes.

_ _ After the accident you were very upset and did all you could for Mr Houghton ?—Yes. A juror: Was there anything else in the road besides this trap ?—No. If you had come straight on, you would have gone through. There was plenty of room ?—Yes. I don't understand what on earth you wanted to put the clutch out for, it there was room and you were not going too fast ?—lt is always usual to put the clutch out when you get in a corner like that. What did you put the brake on for, if there was nothing in the road ?—When the car struck the kerb I didn't know what would happen, so I applied the emergency brake. If I had not done so the car would probably have gone through. I cannot understand what you were doing to strike the kerb if there was nothing in the road.—l suddenly Ea w t'Le trap and in endeavouring to get out of the way and give it as much room as possible, I caught the kerb. The Coroner: This trap suddenly came into your view ?—Yes.

If it had not come into your view, you would have gone with the clutch out, running free engine, along the narrow " bottle neck." ?—Yes. When you saw the trap you thought, " I must give it as much room as I can in this ' bottle neck,'" and you Fulled as much to your near side as you could ?—Yes. In doing so, you pulled the car more to your near side than you really expected to do and your near wheels went on to the kerb ?—Yes. As soon as they struck the kerb you did not know what was going to happen and down you went with your right hand on to the handle of the emergency brake ?—Yes, That left you with the control of the steering entrusted to your left hand alone ?—Yes. The striking of the kerb and the application of the emergency brake caused She car to swerve to the right into the trap ?—Yes. Witness added that there was water in the gutter. The Foreman : Was there any racing between your- self and the motor cyclist ?—None whatever. A motor cyclist can always pass a car—especially mine. Was there any " hurrahing " or particularly jubilant phrases ?—No.

_ A juror : Considering the amount of traffic on the road do you consider it careful riding, if it was necessary to put the brake on and apply the emergency brake —Have the police taken any. steps to ascertain the time it took the car to get from Frodshant to Warrington ? The Chief Constable : The police are not on their trial to answer that question. The Coroner : The police are very probably staying their hand. They are awaiting the result of this inquiry and upon your verdict will moat probably depend what other people wilt (1).

"CAR SLOWED DOWN." Frederick Mullins, assistont manager of the Old House at Home, Friars Green, gave similar evidence. He said the car came down Chester-road at from 16 to 20 miles an hour. When they got near to the " bottle- neck " they slowed down, hit the kerb stone on the loft side of the road, and then collided with the governess car. Witness first saw tha motor cyclist near the Stag Bridge. He was in front of the car.
