The Coroner : Did you overtake him at any point on Chester-road ?—No, not that I know of. What became of tbe motor cycle ?—I cannot say, I did not take particular notice. Did you never overtake it ?—No. Not that I know of.

Were you racing with it ?—No. Mr Ridgway : Was there room for the car to have gone through .—I cannot say that. The Coroner : But you must know whether there was or not. Was Mr Houghton so much cn his near side that if Roberts had gone on without striking the kerbstone, there woulehave been room for the car to go through ?—No, I don't think 9). Well, if be had not caught the kerLslone he would have run into the trap then. Mr Ridgway : When was the trap when you first saw it ?—Just the other side of the lamp post. Close up to the footpah ?—I cannot say. Mr Ridgway : I don't think we shall get much further with him. _ _
Mr Steel Is there Any truth in the statement that you were racing the motor cicls in Chester-road ?—No. Is it true that you shout,d Hurrah ' when you got to the " bottle neck "

Or that the cyclist replied" Hurrah " ?—No. The Chief Constable said be did not think the police could produce any new evidence. There was a great deal of corroboration of the statements of witnesses who said the car was travelling at an excessive speed, tut that was all.

div.head: CORONER SUMS UP.
div.p: THE CORONER SUMS UP.

The Coroner, in summing up,eaid he had had sufficient L experience to know that not only in Warrington but in any town with which be was acq minted, when a case of that kind occured there was always a great deal of gossip and re sour, and many tales fling about. He felt certain that the jury, most of whom he knew very well, would disabuse their minds of all those stories and find their verdict on the evidence given upon oath. Having voiced the general feeling of sorrow at Mr. Houghton's tragic death, the Coroner said that having assumed that the jury wmild find it was due to the collision with the motor car, the next question they had to dec'de was whether Victor Roberts war. in cmascquence of thst collision, responsible for the death of the deceased ? In other words' whether he Lad teen negligent and, if so, in what degree. Anyone going on the road with some- thing dangerous hal duties imposed upon him. As a well-known judge had expressed it, the legal duty of , everyone who did any act whicio, without ordinary pre- cantione, was or might be dangerous to human life, was to employ those precautions in doing it. Roberts had the duty imposed upon him by law of being careful. The only question was: Under the circumstances, did he exercise all the carefulness that the jury would expect him to ? If, under all the circumstances, he was driving with juigment, care, and discretion—in other words, doing everything the jury would do under similar conditione—the affair was a pure accident and nobody was to blame. If on the contrary the jury thought Roberts was neglecting to do something he ought to have done or was doing some- thing he ought not to have done, he had been guilty of negligence. If they came to the cmclusion that he had 1 een negligent, they had the important duty cast upon them of saying whether that negligence MIR censurable or culpable. Many people were negligent in this world and needed reprimands for it. Culpable negligence meant negligence of such a grave degree that to find it meant that it was a criminal negligence and would justify them in sending Roberts for trial for having caused the death of the deceased. In his (the Coroner's) opinion, culpable negligence carried with it reckless indifference to anything that followed. If a man in charge of a vehicle was negli- gent, before the jury could call:that negligence culpable they mats come to the conclusion that it was of such a degree that in the act he was doing he did not care a toss of a button what resulted from it, and was utterly reckless and indifferent as to the consequences. Although the jury had a duty to perform to the relatives of the deceased, the law also said they must not do any injustic3 to the person who was accused. Any doubt there might be in the matter was to be given to the eccused and it was far better that nine guilty persons should escape than that one innocent person should suffer. One witness had stated that the car was going at a terrific speed but when pressed by the Chief Constable as to what he meant by that, he said it was going at 25 miles an hour. To his (the Coroner's) mind, the speed had nothing to do with the dangerous driving of a car. Whereas one car might be driven at a very great speed in the hands of a careful and expert driver and should be quite safe, another might be driven at 10 miles an hour and be absolutely dangerous on account of the ignor- ance of the man at the wheel. It was the expert know- ledge that made the driving of cars not dangerous to the public. One witness described what was absolutely impossible when ho said the car made three movements before colliding with the trap. It would not be in accordance with human nature to expect an exact and accurate account from everybody who witnessed an accident and hence there were discrepancies in the various stories. The evidence of Roberts impressed him (the Coroner) very much after having visited the scene of the acci- dent.Aman must be very able indeed to,drive a car safely with only one hand. The jury had a difficult problem to solve, but if they brought their common sense to bear he did not think they 'could have much difficulty about it. Even assuming Roberts was driving too quickly, even assuming that he was racing the motor cyclist, thoy must have in their minds that when he got to the" bottle neck "he saw the governess car. Was he negligent then in what he did from the River-road up to the time of the accident taking place, or did he do all he possibly could_ußder.the circumstances ?

THE 'VERDICT'. The jury retired to consider their verdict. On their return about twenty minutes later, the fore- man said they found that death occurred in conse- quence of a collision with a motor car, that there was a considerable amount of negligence on the part of Victor G. Roberts, but they did not find that the negligence was of such a serious extent as to be culpable. They did,ihowever, think it WB5l censurable. The jury further thought that in view of the great amount of traffic the Corporation should lose no time in widening the road. It was a veritable death trap and until the read was widened a very prominent notice, calling attention to the danger, should he placed at each end. The jury also wished to express their deep sympathy with Mrs. Houghton and family.

-THE CORONER'S SEVERE CENSURE. Victor Roberts was again called into the box and, in reply to the Coroner, said he was 211 years of age. Addressing Roberts, the C)roner said: You don't mind if I give you some words of friendly advice. I consider that you are a most fortunate person. You yourself must admit the great loss to the community by the deatb, under these sad circumstances, of Mr. Houghton, whom I knew very well as a very respect- able and well-thought-of farmer. I hope that you appreciate that a great deal of sorrow is in the minds of his wife and daughter and everybody belonging to him, On account of his loss. Now I told the jury that they had to decide whether there was negligence on your part or whether that negligence was culpable or not,and I tthhien kwyaoyu irn Solicitorwhichwill aid downadm jury, and that I showed no bias, antipathy or hostility against you. I think the jury, although I do not cons- ththeat proposition I wasntost tfnairthin e ' have en taken a ra t theernciofnuclluvsilsown tnhfatthte naheyahtatevr in saying e come to, that your negligence is culpable. I convey to you whot ' I think about you and your cmduct by saying that it is so near culpable that another inch would have brought it out of censurable negligence into culpable negligence. I know that 3ou are a very able driver and that you know this locality very well. You could nut plead ignorance of the state of the road. You knew this road as well as any other motorist in Warrington. You knew you were coming to a place that the jury themselves say—and I can see for myself and everybody else must acknowledge—is a death trap and absolutely dangerous unless great care is taken, and the obligation rt.sts upon you to take that care. Whether you were racing with this motorcyclist or not is best known to yourself. The only thing I can say is that there is a great volume of evidence to show that you were and there is a great volume of evidence to show that yon were going at a very high rate of speed when you were approaching this "bottle neck." It may be that you lost control when you got into that " bottle neck "and it may be that circumstances arose, over which you had no control, that caused you to run into this governess car. But the jury would not have been doing their duty if they had not found as a fact that there was negligence on your part, and I think the foreman will agree with me when I say they fiad there was very grave havingit h isad y ob caused de cud utlytp, hanb alned deathyotu h new f negligence on your part, but, fortunately for you, they stop there and say that negligence WAS not culpable. If come to stay. They area great convenience both from the pleasure and business standpoints and t otudhluidstyhmanvonef. gel‘ovienaretynfrorntart an trial for have drives a car, to see that you do not irritate omrannw" ly, let alone injure the public in driving your car. You are doing not only a wrong to wrong to doing as you did on this day, because you are bringing your colleagues who drive motor cars by so yourself but a great the whole driving of motor cars into disrepute and , discredit. You are a young man. I hope this will be I a very great lesson to you. If this life is not on your mind legally, it is on your mind morally, and if I were in your place I should rertrA up to the moment I went into the grave that I bad any act:that had brought about this death. You are not guiltless. There was very grave negligence on your part. Let me beg of you to let it be a lesson to you.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday. Mr. Linaker presiding. GRAPPENHALL SEWERAGE SCHEME. The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Lister Kaye, asking if the Council could not see their way to defer the Grappenhall sewerage scheme in its entirety or submit I a modified scheme. He pointed out that the scheme would meet with opposition. In the course of a lengthy discussion which the reporters were required not to note it was stated that the entire cost of the scheme was £lB,OOO for the three parishes. The Clerk was requested to write to Mr. Kaye point- ing out that the scheme could not be withdrawn and explaining the circumstances. THE DOCTOR'S REPORT. Dr. Nicholls was called upon to give the doctor's report and said be understood that during the absence of Dr. AdaMS be was to fulfil the duties as medical officer of health and submit reports. The Clerk said he had asked Dr. Adams if he would submit a report and he Lad said Dr. Nicholls would act in his absence. The Doctor reported two cases of scarlet fever and one of enteric end he had acted according to the usual custom in the matter.
